steps.answer: Dividing the work would require the causes to differ — this one doing that job, that one doing this — and steps 15 and 16 show there is no feature available to tell them apart. So there is not even in principle room for more than one, and everything traces back to the same actualizer.

steps.text: To be capable of change, the purely actual actualizer would need potentials that could be actualized.
steps.why: Change just is the actualization of potential (step 2).
steps.example: For the purely actual actualizer to change, it would have to be able to go from being one way to being another — that is, it would have to have some potential sitting there waiting to be actualized.
steps.challenge: Isn’t that definition of change too narrow? Surely something could change in some other sense of the word.
steps.answer: Step 2 already fixed what change is: the actualization of a potential — and that account was defended on its own merits, as Aristotle’s answer to Parmenides, long before God entered the discussion. Anything called change that does not fit that description is simply a different subject.

steps.text: But because it is purely actual, it has no such potentials.
steps.why: That is what ‘purely actual’ means: no unrealized potential whatsoever.
steps.example: “Purely actual” means exactly this: not one single respect in which the thing could be brought to be some way it currently isn’t.
steps.challenge: Isn’t it suspicious that the very definition used to stop the regress then hands over every divine attribute for free?
steps.answer: That is the argument’s design rather than a trick. Stage 1 argues on independent grounds that the regress must end in something with no unactualized potential; Stage 2 then just spells out what such a thing would have to be like. Anyone who wants to block the attributes has to attack the Stage 1 reasoning, not the bookkeeping here.

steps.text: So it is immutable — incapable of change.
steps.why: From 19 and 20.
steps.example: The purely actual actualizer cannot cool down, grow, move, learn, age or decay — not because it is frozen stiff, but because there is nothing in it left to be brought about.
steps.challenge: An unchanging God sounds inert. How could such a thing act in the world, create, or respond to anyone?
steps.answer: Feser notes that actualizing something else does not require changing yourself — that assumption comes from the only actualizers we have met, which have to change because they are limited mixtures of act and potency (your arm can move the stick to a new spot only because the arm itself goes from being actually here to actually there). Something with no such limitation can actualize without undergoing anything. He treats divine action at length in his later chapter on the divine attributes.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer existed in time, it would be capable of change — which it is not.
steps.why: Existing in time entails changeability (moving from one moment to the next, having a before and after); step 21 rules changeability out.
steps.example: To exist in time is to have a before and an after — to be one way at one moment and another way at the next, which is just to be changeable.
steps.challenge: Couldn’t it exist in time and simply never happen to change — everlasting rather than timeless?
steps.answer: The claim is stronger than “it never changes”: existing in time entails being *capable* of change, and step 21 ruled out the capability, not merely its exercise. So what follows is timelessness rather than unlimited duration.

steps.text: So it is eternal, existing outside time altogether.
steps.why: From 21 and 22. ‘Eternal’ here means timeless — without beginning, end, or succession — not merely everlasting.
steps.example: “Eternal” here does not mean lasting a very long time, or even lasting forever. It means standing outside the run of moments altogether — no beginning, no end, no before and after within it.
steps.challenge: A timeless being seems unable to do anything at all, since every action happens at some time.
steps.answer: The timing belongs to the effect, not to the cause: the water is being held in being at this moment, but nothing in the cause has to move from one moment to the next for that to be true. Feser flags that the full defence of divine eternity belongs to his later chapter on the divine attributes.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer were material, it would be changeable and in time — which it is not.
steps.why: Being material entails being changeable and temporal; steps 21 and 23 exclude both.
steps.example: Anything made of matter can be heated, dented, moved or broken apart, and it has a history running through time — which is to say it carries potentials waiting to be actualized.
steps.challenge: Physics keeps finding that matter is far stranger than common sense suggests; maybe some exotic form of matter isn’t changeable in the relevant way.
steps.answer: The step does not depend on any particular physics. Whatever matter turns out to be, being material means being the kind of thing that could be otherwise — and that is exactly a mixture of actuality and potentiality, which pure actuality excludes. Feser makes the same point when he answers the “outdated science” objection: the specific physical details affect how we apply act and potency, not whether we must.

steps.text: So it is immaterial.
steps.why: From 21, 23 and 24.
steps.example: Being immaterial here does not mean being made of some thin ghostly stuff. It means not being made of anything that could have been otherwise.
steps.challenge: An immaterial cause is unobservable in principle — precisely the sort of thing we have no business believing in.
steps.answer: This is Kant’s worry, and Feser answers that although we learn the principle of causality from experience, what the principle rests on is not experience but the fact that a potential cannot actualize itself — and that holds quite generally. His comparison: we learn geometry from figures drawn in black ink, but what we learn applies to figures of any colour and of no colour at all.

steps.text: If it were corporeal (had a body), it would be material — which it is not.
steps.why: Having a body entails being material.
steps.example: A body is a parcel of matter with a size and a location. Anything with one is material, and so inherits everything that follows from being material.
steps.challenge: Some traditions do picture God with a body, or identify God with the physical universe itself.
steps.answer: Both are excluded by the same reasoning rather than by preference: having a body means being material, and being material brings changeability and existence in time with it — which steps 21 and 23 have already ruled out for a purely actual cause.

steps.text: So it is incorporeal.
steps.why: From 25 and 26.
steps.example: The purely actual actualizer has no shape, no size, no location and no parts to be pushed around.

steps.text: If the purely actual actualizer were imperfect in any respect, it would have some unactualized potential — which it does not.
steps.why: Imperfection is a privation: failing to realize a potential proper to one’s nature (the injured squirrel, the tree with damaged roots).
steps.example: A squirrel hit by a car can no longer outrun predators; a tree with damaged roots cannot draw the water it needs. Each falls short of something its own nature called for — a privation, which is simply a potential left unrealized.
steps.challenge: Calling it “perfect” sounds like a compliment smuggled into a metaphysical argument.
steps.answer: Feser is using perfection in a strictly metaphysical sense: a thing is perfect to the extent that it has actualized the potentials proper to it and has no privations. Something with no unactualized potential whatsoever is therefore perfect in that sense automatically, with no praise implied.

steps.text: So it is perfect.
steps.why: From 20 and 28.
steps.example: Nothing can be missing from a thing that has no potential left to realize — there is no gap in it for a defect to sit in.

steps.text: To be less than fully good is to have a privation — to fail to actualize some feature proper to oneself.
steps.why: A thing is good insofar as it realizes the potentials of its kind and bad insofar as it doesn’t (the good vs. the bad painter).
steps.example: A bad painter is bad because he never acquired the craftsmanship, composition and skill the art calls for; a good painter is good because he has. Goodness in this general sense is a matter of realizing what your kind of thing is for.
steps.challenge: This makes goodness a matter of functioning well, which has nothing to do with moral goodness — so calling the cause “fully good” is a bait and switch.
steps.answer: Feser is explicit that he means goodness in a general, metaphysical sense at this stage of the book, and that the personal and moral implications need separate argument, which he supplies in his later chapter on the divine attributes. The step itself claims only that falling short of full goodness means lacking something you could have had.

steps.text: Being purely actual, the purely actual actualizer can have no privation.
steps.why: A privation is an unactualized potential, and it has none.
steps.example: A privation is a hole in a thing — some potential proper to it that has never been realized, like the squirrel’s lost speed or the tree’s ruined roots. Pure actuality has no holes, because it has no unrealized potentials to begin with.
steps.challenge: Then what about evil? If the source of everything is fully good, the world’s suffering looks like evidence against it.
steps.answer: The problem of evil is an objection to where the argument arrives, not to this step: here “good” means having no privation, and a purely actual actualizer has none by construction. Feser postpones evil and the divine attributes to a later chapter rather than answering them in this one.

steps.text: So it is fully good.
steps.why: From 30 and 31.
steps.example: The purely actual actualizer is not good in a competitive sense, as a good painter is better than a bad one. It is a thing with nothing at all lacking in it.

steps.text: Having power means being able to actualize potentials.
steps.why: Power is just the ability to make something happen, i.e., to actualize a potential.
steps.example: Lighting a match, lifting a cup, warming a room, cooling coffee — in each case having power means nothing more than being able to bring about something that was until then only possible.
steps.challenge: That defines power so broadly that anything which does anything has it, so nothing about God follows yet.
steps.answer: Quite so — this step is only a definition, and it is meant to be uncontroversial. The work is done by step 34, which locates where every such ability ultimately comes from.

steps.text: Every potential that gets actualized is actualized either by the purely actual actualizer directly or by a series of actualizers that ends in it.
steps.why: This is the upshot of Stage 1: every actualizer is either pure act or depends, here and now, on a hierarchical series terminating in pure act — and there is only one such (step 18).
steps.example: The room’s air cools the coffee, the air conditioner cooled the air, the power station drives the air conditioner — and every one of those actualizers exists at this moment only because the purely actual actualizer is holding it in being at this moment.
steps.challenge: This simply recycles Stage 1; if Stage 1 fails, this collapses with it.
steps.answer: That is true, and Feser does not hide it: Stage 2 draws out the consequences of there being a purely actual actualizer, so it stands or falls with Stage 1. The extra work here is done by the unity result of step 18, which makes it one source of power rather than many.

steps.text: So all power derives from the purely actual actualizer.
steps.why: From 33 and 34: all actualizing traces back to it, so every power anything has is derived from it.
steps.example: Every ability anything has to make anything happen is, in the end, on loan from the same lender.

steps.text: To be the source from which all power derives is to be omnipotent.
steps.why: A being that is the source of every possible actualizing power, and is pure actuality itself rather than one actual thing among others, has all power.
steps.example: The purely actual actualizer is not one powerful thing among others, drawing on a supply of power; it is actuality itself, the source from which every actualizing power anything has is derived.
steps.challenge: The classic puzzle: could it make a stone too heavy for it to lift, or make a contradiction true?
steps.answer: Omnipotence here means being the source of all actualizing power, not being able to perform describable nonsense — “a stone too heavy for an unlimited power to lift” names no possible task at all. Feser flags that a careful treatment of omnipotence belongs to his later chapter on the divine attributes.

steps.text: So it is omnipotent.
steps.why: From 35 and 36.
steps.example: All power derives from it, and being that from which all power derives is what omnipotence amounts to.

steps.text: Whatever is in an effect is in its cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently (the principle of proportionate causality).
steps.why: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have. The $20 example: I may have the bill in hand (formally), have access to it via the bank (virtually), or have the power to print twenties (eminently).
steps.example: To give you $20 I must have it somehow: a bill in my wallet (formally), credit in my bank account I can draw on (virtually), or the legal power to have twenties printed (eminently). What I cannot do is hand over what I have in none of those ways.
steps.challenge: Causes obviously produce things they don’t contain — a fire produces smoke but isn’t smoky, and parents produce a child who isn’t a copy of them.
steps.answer: That is exactly why the principle allows three ways of having: the fire has smoke virtually, in its power to produce it. The principle says only that a cause cannot give what it has in no way at all — which is why nobody expects a struck match to produce a symphony.

steps.text: The purely actual actualizer is the cause of all things.
steps.why: From Stage 1 and step 18: it is what actualizes the existence of everything that exists.
steps.example: Cats, trees, stones, galaxies, people — every one of them exists at this instant only because this one cause is holding it in being (steps 13, 14 and 18).
steps.challenge: Perhaps it sustains only the deepest layer of reality, and everything above that layer is built up by ordinary causes.
steps.answer: On Feser’s reasoning no layer escapes: anything with a potential for existence needs actualizing here and now, and every such chain runs back to the same terminus. Ordinary causes are perfectly real, but they operate as instruments inside those chains rather than as replacements for them.

steps.text: So the forms or patterns found in all the things it causes must somehow be in it.
steps.why: From 38 and 39: to cause a thing is to cause something of a definite kind (a stone, not a tree), so the cause must possess those forms in some way.
steps.example: To hold a cat in being is not to hold a vague blur in being — it is to hold *this kind of thing* in being rather than a stone or a tree. So whatever makes a cat be a cat has to be present in its cause in some way.
steps.challenge: Why must the pattern itself be in the cause, rather than merely the power to produce things of that kind?
steps.answer: Having the power to produce things of that kind is already one of the three ways of having it — virtually or eminently rather than formally. The step claims only that the pattern is in the cause somehow, not that the cause is furry.

steps.text: Forms can exist in one of two ways: concretely, as in individual things, or abstractly, as in the thoughts of an intellect.
steps.why: A material triangle has triangularity by being a triangle; a mind has it by thinking of triangularity without becoming a triangle.
steps.example: A wooden triangle has triangularity by *being* a triangle. Your mind has triangularity when you think about what it is to be a triangle — without your head becoming three-sided. Those are the two ways a pattern can be had.
steps.challenge: Aren’t there other options — forms existing in language, in mathematics, or in some Platonic realm of their own?
steps.answer: Feser is drawing the distinction that the argument needs: a form is either instantiated in a concrete individual or held abstractly, apart from any particular instance. Words and equations are themselves either concrete marks on paper or things held in thought, so they do not supply a third, independent way.

steps.text: The forms cannot exist in the purely actual actualizer the way they exist in individual things.
steps.why: It is immaterial and one (steps 18, 25); it is not itself a cat or a tree. Also, as the cause of every possible instance of each form, it must have the forms universally, not as this or that particular.
steps.example: The cause of every possible cat is not itself a cat: it is immaterial (step 25) and one (step 18), and it has to have catness in a way that covers every possible cat, not just the particular one on your mat.
steps.challenge: Maybe the cause has the forms in some third way we simply cannot imagine.
steps.answer: Feser’s move is elimination among the ways a form can exist, and the concrete way is closed off by results already secured — the cause is immaterial, and it must relate to every possible instance universally rather than to this or that particular. A third way would have to be described and defended, not merely gestured at.

steps.text: So they exist in it abstractly, in the way forms exist in the thoughts of an intellect.
steps.why: From 40, 41 and 42 by elimination.
steps.example: The pattern of every possible cat, tree and stone is present in the cause the way triangularity is present in a mind contemplating triangles: universally, abstracted from any particular instance.
steps.challenge: Saying the forms are in it “like thoughts” may be a helpful image rather than an argument.
steps.answer: The step rests on the two-way distinction of step 41 plus the elimination of step 42, not on how attractive the picture is. The structural point is what matters: having a form universally, rather than by being an instance of it, is precisely what having it abstractly means.

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer has intellect — it is intelligent.
steps.why: Having forms abstractly or universally is the core capacity of intellect. And since it also causes the relations among things (all men being mortal, this cat being on this mat), these pre-exist in it as combinations of forms — i.e., as thoughts, like a craftsman’s plans.
steps.example: A craftsman has the vase in mind before it exists in clay. On this reasoning the patterns of everything that could exist pre-exist in the purely actual cause in something like that way — including their combinations, such as all men being mortal, or this cat being on this mat.
steps.challenge: Intelligence as we know it involves consciousness, a brain, and learning things you didn’t know before; calling this cause “intelligent” stretches the word past recognition.
steps.answer: Feser defines intelligence by its three capacities — grasping universal concepts, combining them into complete thoughts, and inferring one thought from others — with the first as the most fundamental, and none of the three requires a brain or a process of learning. He is explicit that this is only a sketch, with the full account of divine intellect reserved for his later chapter.

steps.text: Since the forms of all things are in this intellect’s thoughts, nothing lies outside the range of those thoughts.
steps.why: It causes everything that exists or could exist, so every form and every combination of forms is in it.
steps.example: There is no possible cat, no possible arrangement of matter, and no possible fact about how such things are related that falls outside the range of a cause that is causing every possible form and every possible combination of forms.
steps.challenge: Could it know things that are not forms or combinations of forms — what pain feels like, say, or what a free creature will choose?
steps.answer: Feser’s sketch here stays at the level of forms and their combinations, because that is what the principle of proportionate causality delivers. Knowledge of particulars and of free acts he explicitly defers to his later chapter on the divine attributes.

steps.text: For nothing to lie outside the range of something’s thoughts is for that thing to be omniscient.
steps.why: A definition of omniscience.
steps.example: Omniscience means there is nothing left over — no fact standing outside what this cause knows.
steps.challenge: This is a stipulated definition; someone could define omniscience differently and the conclusion would change.
steps.answer: It is the standard definition, and the argument uses it only to put a familiar name on what step 45 has already established. If you prefer a different word, the substance is untouched: nothing that exists or could exist lies outside the range of this cause’s thoughts.

steps.text: So the purely actual actualizer is omniscient.
steps.why: From 45 and 46.
steps.example: Nothing that exists or could exist falls outside its knowledge, and that is what it is to be all-knowing.

steps.text: So there exists a purely actual cause of the existence of things that is one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, fully good, omnipotent, intelligent and omniscient.
steps.example: One immaterial, timeless, changeless, perfect, fully good, all-powerful, intelligent and all-knowing cause is keeping your coffee cup — and everything else — in existence at this very instant.
steps.challenge: This is a chain of eleven separate sub-arguments; if any one of them fails, the whole description of the cause collapses.
steps.answer: Feser is candid that Stage 2 is a sketch and that objections to the divine attributes get a whole chapter of their own later in the book. But the attributes are not independent add-ons bolted together: every one of them is derived from the same single feature — having no unactualized potential — so they stand or fall with Stage 1 rather than one at a time.

steps.text: For such a cause of things to exist is exactly what it is for God to exist.
steps.why: These are the defining attributes of God as traditionally conceived, and God is, whatever else he is, the ultimate cause of things — here, the cause that keeps them in being at every moment.
steps.example: What people mean by God is not merely some very powerful being, but the ultimate cause of things — and here that means the cause keeping everything in being at every moment it exists.
steps.challenge: This is the God of the philosophers, not the God of any living religion: no love, no revelation, no commandments.
steps.answer: Feser’s claim at this point is that the argument already delivers far more than a bare first cause — unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence, intellect and omniscience — which is the traditional description of God, not a generic something. He readily grants that much more must be said, and devotes a whole later chapter to the divine attributes.

steps.text: Therefore God exists.
steps.why: From 48 and 49.
steps.example: If every step holds, then the thing whose existence has just been demonstrated is what the classical tradition has always meant by the word God.

keyTerms.definition: The actualization of a potential: what was potentially F becomes actually F. Aristotelians call change in general ‘motion’, so ‘mover’ and ‘moved’ mean ‘actualizer’ and ‘actualized’.
keyTerms.example: Hot coffee, which is potentially cold, becomes actually cold as the room’s cool air acts on it.
keyTerms.origin: Greek kinēsis and metabolē; Latin motus. Aristotle defines change in Physics III as the actualization of what is potential, precisely as potential.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Motion in the modern, narrow sense of change of place. For Aristotelians ‘motion’ covers every kind of change, not just movement through space.

keyTerms.definition: The way a thing actually is here and now — its realized features. Only what is actual can do anything. Related forms: ‘actual’, ‘actualize’ (to make actual), ‘actualization’.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s actual heat, and the actual coolness of the room’s air that takes the heat away.
keyTerms.origin: Greek energeia (‘being-at-work’) and entelecheia (‘being-at-completion’); Latin actus. Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being ‘real’. Potentials are real too; actuality is realized being, as opposed to a real but unrealized capacity.

keyTerms.definition: A real but unrealized capacity of a thing to be or become some way. Not nothing, and not yet actual: a determinate range of what this thing can become, which excludes other possibilities. Traditional synonym: ‘potency’.
keyTerms.example: Coffee can grow cold and can stain the carpet; it cannot become chicken soup or a live chicken. Those limits are what show that its coldness is already there potentially.
keyTerms.origin: Greek dynamis (‘power, capacity’); Latin potentia. Aristotle. Heisenberg borrowed the same word, potentia, for the objective tendencies quantum theory describes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility. A potential is a specific capacity rooted in a thing’s nature, not everything one can imagine without contradiction.

keyTerms.definition: The ancient argument that change is impossible, because what comes into being (say, the coffee’s coldness) would have to come from nothing, and nothing comes from nothing.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s coldness seems to spring from nowhere while the coffee is hot, so Parmenides concludes that the cooling cannot really happen.
keyTerms.origin: Parmenides of Elea (early fifth century BC), in his poem dividing the Way of Truth from the Way of Opinion.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Zeno’s paradoxes. Zeno, Parmenides’ disciple, attacked motion with puzzles about infinite divisibility; Parmenides argued that being cannot come from non-being.

keyTerms.definition: Qualitative (a quality alters), local (place alters), quantitative (size or amount alters) and substantial (one kind of thing gives way to another). The first three are accidental changes: the same substance persists through them.
keyTerms.example: Coffee cooling (qualitative); a leaf falling (local); a puddle growing (quantitative); a swatted fly becoming dead matter (substantial).
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle (Physics, Categories): alloiōsis (alteration), phora (locomotion), auxēsis and phthisis (growth and diminution), genesis and phthora (generation and corruption).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Substantial with accidental change. The cooled coffee is still coffee; the swatted fly is no longer a fly.

keyTerms.definition: No potential can be actualized except by something already actual. It follows from what potentiality is, not from a survey of observed regularities. Often abbreviated PC; it is step 4 of the formal argument.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s potential coldness cannot make itself actual, because what is merely potential cannot do anything; something already cool — the room’s air, or ice — has to do it.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian and scholastic. Aquinas’ First Way states it as ‘whatever is moved is moved by another’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Everything has a cause’, and the principle of sufficient reason (PSR, the broader Leibnizian claim that everything has an explanation). PC covers only what goes from potential to actual — which is exactly why ‘What caused God?’ misses it.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever actualizes a potential in something else. It need not be changing itself; the rule is only that if it is changing, its own change needs an actualizer.
keyTerms.example: The air conditioner actualizes the air’s potential to be cool, and the cool air actualizes the coffee’s potential to be cold.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s ‘mover’ (to kinoun); ‘actualizer’ is Feser’s wording, chosen because it is not tied to change of place.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A cause that must itself be changing. Feser flags this explicitly: nothing said in the argument implies that every changer is changing.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes strung out through time in which each member has its causal power on its own, relative to the others, so it keeps acting after earlier members are gone. Also called ‘accidentally ordered’. Feser grants that such a series might have no first member.
keyTerms.example: You press the button, the air conditioner cools the air, the air cools the coffee — and the air conditioner keeps cooling even after you leave the house.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per accidens, ‘incidentally’; the scholastic phrase is causes ordered per accidens (Aquinas, Duns Scotus). Feser gives the equivalence in a footnote.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Accidental’ in the sense of ‘random’. It means only that the ordering is not essential to each member’s power to act.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which every member except the first has its causal power only derivatively, as an instrument, and acts only while it is being acted on by an earlier member. Also called ‘essentially ordered’. It must have a first member.
keyTerms.example: The earth holds up the foundation, which holds up the floor, which holds up the desk, which holds up the cup. Pull out the floor and everything above it falls at once.
keyTerms.origin: Latin per se, ‘through itself’ or ‘essentially’; causes ordered per se (Aquinas, Duns Scotus).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A merely simultaneous series. Simultaneity is how Feser introduces the idea, but the defining mark is derivative, instrumental causal power.

keyTerms.definition: A cause whose power to produce the effect is borrowed, and is exercised only while something else acts through it. The opposite is underived, inherent, ‘built-in’ power.
keyTerms.example: The brush does not paint the picture; the painter paints with it. The desk does not hold up the cup on its own; the earth holds it up through the desk.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa instrumentalis, contrasted with causa principalis, the principal cause.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An unimportant cause. An instrument can be indispensable — no painting without a brush — and still have no power of its own to produce the effect.

keyTerms.definition: A cause with underived, built-in causal power: one that can actualize without being actualized. ‘First’ means first in rank or in the order of dependence, not earliest in time or first in a count.
keyTerms.example: The painter, relative to brush and paint. Feser adds that even the earth is not first in the strict sense, because its own existence is being actualized too.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s prōton kinoun, ‘first mover’; scholastic causa prima.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The temporally first cause — whatever set off the Big Bang. Feser’s first cause would be needed even in a universe that never began.

keyTerms.definition: What has no potentiality whatever, and therefore needs no actualizer and could not have one. It does not merely have actuality; it is actuality. Adjective: ‘purely actual’. Latin: actus purus.
keyTerms.example: Everything in our experience is a mixture: coffee actually hot but potentially cold, your arm actually here but potentially there. Take away every ‘but potentially’ and what is left is pure act.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus; rooted in Aristotle’s Metaphysics XII and developed by Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A supremely powerful being, or the greatest item on the list of things that exist — pure act is not one actual thing among many. Note too that it is uncaused, not self-caused: a cause of itself would have to exist before itself, which is incoherent.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that actualizes other things without being actualized. Feser argues it must be unmovable — incapable of being actualized at all — and not merely unmoved as a matter of fact.
keyTerms.example: Whatever is holding the water in your coffee in existence at this instant, without anything holding it in existence in turn.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle’s first unmoved mover (Physics VIII; Metaphysics XII). ‘Unactualized actualizer’ is Feser’s more precise restatement.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mover that merely happens not to be moved. Feser devotes a whole section (‘Why an unmovable mover?’) to closing that gap.

keyTerms.definition: A cause of a thing’s continuing to exist here and now, as opposed to whatever originally produced it. The Aristotelian proof is ultimately about sustaining causes.
keyTerms.example: Not the brewing that made the coffee, but whatever makes this matter exist as water right now rather than as separate hydrogen and oxygen.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic causa essendi (cause of being) as against causa fiendi (cause of becoming); Aquinas on divine conservation.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The originating cause. ‘Someone brewed it’ answers a different question from ‘what keeps it in being?’

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s analysis of a material substance as a composite of substantial form (what makes it the kind of thing it is and unifies its matter) and prime matter (sheer potential to take on form, with no features of its own). Also spelled hylomorphism.
keyTerms.example: Water is not a heap of atoms: on this view the atoms exist in it only ‘virtually’, and its real constituents are substantial form and prime matter.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hylē (‘matter, wood’) plus morphē (‘form, shape’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Atomism, which treats a body as an aggregate of particles. Feser’s footnote restates the proof hylemorphically: form and matter each depend on the other, so something outside the composite must keep it in being.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of something a thing’s own nature requires for completeness — a potential proper to it left unrealized. Imperfection and badness are privations.
keyTerms.example: A squirrel hit by a car that can no longer outrun predators; a tree whose damaged roots cannot take in enough water.
keyTerms.origin: Greek sterēsis; Latin privatio. Aristotle, later applied to evil by Augustine and Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere negation. A stone’s lack of sight is a negation, since sight is not proper to stones; a blind dog’s lack of sight is a privation.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a thing has actualized the potentials proper to it and is free of privation. What is purely actual has maximal perfection (steps 28–29).
keyTerms.example: A healthy, fully grown oak is more perfect as an oak than a stunted, diseased one.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, ‘thoroughly made, completed’ (per + facere).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral flawlessness. In the metaphysical sense, perfection is completeness of any kind.

keyTerms.definition: A thing is good so far as it realizes the potentials belonging to it as the kind of thing it is, and bad so far as it fails to. Having no privation at all, pure actuality is fully good (steps 30–32).
keyTerms.example: A good painter is one who has realized his potential for craftsmanship and composition; a bad painter has failed to acquire the skills.
keyTerms.origin: The Aristotelian–Thomistic account of natural goodness: good as the fulfilment of a thing’s nature.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral goodness. Step 32 claims only that a purely actual cause lacks no perfection proper to it; the problem of evil targets moral goodness, which Feser takes up in later chapters.

keyTerms.definition: There can be only one purely actual cause, because telling two apart would require a differentiating feature, and any such feature would mean a potential or a privation in one of them (steps 15–18).
keyTerms.example: Two trees differ in height, location, sturdiness of roots. Nothing of that sort is available to distinguish two purely actual causes, which are immaterial, eternal and without privation.
keyTerms.origin: The classical divine attribute of oneness; Latin unitas, with unicitas used for there being only one.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine simplicity — having no parts or composition of any kind. Simplicity also follows from pure actuality, but Feser defends it in later chapters, not here.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its cause in some way — formally, virtually or eminently — because a cause cannot give what it does not have. Often abbreviated PPC; it is step 38.
keyTerms.example: I can give you $20 only if I have it somehow: a bill in my wallet, credit in my bank account, or the power to have the bills made.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic maxim, usually put as nemo dat quod non habet, ‘no one gives what he does not have’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality. PC says that an actualizer is needed; PPC says what the actualizer must already contain. Stage 2 needs PPC; Stage 1 did not.

keyTerms.definition: Three ways a cause can ‘have’ what turns up in its effect: formally (it has the very same feature), virtually (it has the power to get hold of it), eminently (it has it in a higher way, such as the power to make such things exist in the first place).
keyTerms.example: A $20 bill in the wallet (formally); $20 of credit in the bank (virtually); authority to print twenties (eminently).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic Latin formaliter, virtualiter, eminenter; Descartes uses the formal/eminent pair in Meditation III.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Assuming ‘in the cause’ must mean ‘in the cause in the same way’. Only the formal mode requires that — which is why the cause of cats need not be a cat.

keyTerms.definition: The capacity to grasp universal concepts, combine them into thoughts, and reason from thought to thought. Its core is having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing. Feser uses ‘intellect’ and ‘intelligence’ interchangeably here.
keyTerms.example: You grasp what it is to be a triangle without becoming a triangle, and your concept of man applies to every man who could exist.
keyTerms.origin: Greek nous; Latin intellectus, from intellegere, ‘to understand’. Medieval writers liked to gloss it as intus legere, ‘to read within’, though that is a pious gloss rather than the real derivation.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Imagination or sensation. Images are always particular — you cannot picture a thousand-sided figure distinctly — while the intellect grasps the universal.

keyTerms.definition: What makes a thing the kind of thing it is. The same form can exist concretely in individual things or abstractly in an intellect, which is the hinge of steps 40–44.
keyTerms.example: The pattern shared by all triangles: it exists in drawn triangles, and it exists in you when you think about triangles in general.
keyTerms.origin: Greek eidos or morphē; Latin forma. Plato and Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere shape. Form includes shape but means the whole organizing nature that makes a thing what it is.

keyTerms.definition: Two of Aristotle’s four causes (the others, material and final, play no role in this chapter). The formal cause is a thing’s nature or form, which grounds how it behaves; the efficient cause is what produces or sustains it.
keyTerms.example: Lead-210’s nature grounds its probability of decaying (formal cause); whatever generated the atom, and whatever keeps it in existence now, are efficient causes.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Physics II and Metaphysics V.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The modern habit of hearing ‘cause’ as efficient cause only. Feser’s reply to the radioactive-decay objection depends on counting a thing’s nature as a genuine cause.

keyTerms.definition: Physics’ method of describing only those aspects of nature that can be captured mathematically. This is why it is so precise, and also why it is guaranteed to leave out qualitative and causal features — including actuality and potentiality.
keyTerms.example: A metal detector finds only metal; its silence about wood is a fact about the detector, not about the room. A black-and-white drawing likewise omits colour that is really in the scene.
keyTerms.origin: C. B. Martin’s terms, quoted by Feser; the method itself goes back to Galileo and Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A temporary gap that future physics will fill. The omission is built into the method, so no future physics removes it. Russell conceded the same point from the other side: physics gives the structure of events and is silent about their intrinsic character.

keyTerms.definition: Minkowski’s four-dimensional reading of relativity, on which past, present and future are all equally real, so that change is (allegedly) illusory. Feser calls it a picture of actuality without potentiality.
keyTerms.example: Moments of time treated like places on a map, all equally ‘there’, with the passing of time a feature of our experience only.
keyTerms.origin: Hermann Minkowski’s 1908 geometrical formulation of special relativity; the view is also called eternalism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Relativity itself. The block universe is one philosophical interpretation of relativity, and physicists such as Lee Smolin reject it.

keyTerms.definition: Treating a merely contingent feature of the cases you happen to have met as though it belonged to the kind essentially.
keyTerms.example: Every U.S. president so far has been under seven feet tall; it does not follow that no seven-footer could be president. Likewise every actualizer we have met changes, but that need not be essential to actualizing.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations; Latin fallacia accidentis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hasty generalization. They are close cousins, but this fallacy specifically promotes an accidental feature into an essential one.

keyTerms.definition: Exempting one case from a rule you apply to everything else, with no principled reason for the exemption.
keyTerms.example: Demanding evidence from rival theories that you never demand of your own. Feser answers that his exemption is not like this: things need causes because they have potentials, and pure act has none.
keyTerms.origin: From legal usage, where ‘special pleading’ originally meant a plea introducing new matter; it came to mean arguing only the side that suits you.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled exception. An exception is special pleading only when the rule’s own rationale does not cover it.

keyTerms.definition: Being incapable of change, because there is no potential left to be actualized (steps 19–21). Adjective: ‘immutable’; opposite: ‘mutable’.
keyTerms.example: Coffee can cool, a leaf can fall, the earth can shift — each has potentials waiting. A purely actual cause has none, so nothing about it could ever be otherwise.
keyTerms.origin: Latin immutabilis, ‘unchangeable’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or lifelessness. Immutability here is fullness of act, not frozen passivity: the immutable cause is the source of all activity.

keyTerms.definition: Existing outside time altogether — no beginning, no end, no succession — rather than lasting through all time (steps 22–23). Adjective: ‘eternal’.
keyTerms.example: Anything in time can change, since it can be one way now and another later; so a cause that cannot change cannot be in time at all.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas. Boethius’ classic definition is the complete and simultaneous possession of unlimited life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness (sempiternity) — existing at every moment of an endless time. That is still being in time.

keyTerms.definition: Not made of matter, and therefore not having a body of any kind (steps 24–27). Opposites: ‘material’ and ‘corporeal’.
keyTerms.example: Matter is changeable and exists in time; a purely actual cause is neither, so it cannot be material, and so cannot be bodily either.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- (‘not’) with materia (‘matter’) and corpus (‘body’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being invisible, or made of some thin stuff like gas or ‘energy’. Those are still material; immaterial means not material at all.

keyTerms.definition: Having all power: being the source of every actualizing power anything has, and so able to actualize any potential (steps 33–37). Adjective: ‘omnipotent’.
keyTerms.example: Every actualization traces either directly to the purely actual actualizer or through a series of actualizers ending in it, so all power is derived from it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) plus potens (‘able, powerful’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The ability to do the logically impossible. Power is the ability to actualize potentials, and a square circle is not a potential of anything.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing everything: nothing that exists or could exist falls outside the range of this intellect’s thoughts (steps 45–47). Adjective: ‘omniscient’.
keyTerms.example: Because the forms of every possible thing are in the cause of all things, there is nothing left over for it not to know.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) plus scientia (‘knowledge’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Knowledge gathered by observation. On this argument the cause knows things the way a maker knows a plan, not by learning from them.

keyTerms.definition: A position that undermines itself, because holding it or arguing for it requires the very thing it denies.
keyTerms.example: Arguing that change is unreal: your mind has to move from premise to premise to conclusion, and that is itself a change.
keyTerms.origin: A classic retort since antiquity (Greek peritropē, ‘turning the tables’), used against radical skeptics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Circular reasoning. A circular argument assumes its own conclusion; a self-refuting one contradicts its own presuppositions.

keyTerms.definition: Rejecting a claim or argument because of facts about the person making it — their motives, say — rather than on its merits.
keyTerms.example: Claiming that the potential-to-actual formulation must be false because theists supposedly adopted it to dodge ‘What caused God?’.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hominem, ‘to the person’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Questioning a witness’s reliability, which can be relevant to testimony but is irrelevant to whether an argument’s premises are true and its logic valid.

keyTerms.definition: Inferring that a whole has some property just because each of its parts has it.
keyTerms.example: Every brick in a wall is small, so the wall is small. Critics level this charge at first-cause arguments; Feser answers that his argument reasons about each thing individually and never about the universe as a whole.
keyTerms.origin: Traditional logic; Aristotle treats fallacies of composition and division in Sophistical Refutations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Applying a principle to each member of a class one by one, which is not a fallacy at all.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming in the premises the very conclusion that is in dispute.
keyTerms.example: Sobel’s charge that calling intermediate causes ‘instrumental’ already assumes a first cause; and Feser’s countercharge that ‘every actualizer must itself change’ simply assumes that pure act is impossible.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’, translating Aristotle’s phrase for asking to be granted the point at issue.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Raising the question’, as in popular usage. In logic the phrase names a specific fallacy.

keyTerms.definition: The view that all knowledge derives from sense experience. Hume is its most famous skeptical exponent. A holder of the view is an ‘empiricist’; ‘empirical’ means based on observation.
keyTerms.example: Hume’s case against the principle of causality runs on empiricist assumptions about what our being able to imagine something shows.
keyTerms.origin: Greek empeiria (‘experience’); Locke, Berkeley and Hume.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science. One can accept science entirely without accepting the philosophical thesis that only sense experience yields knowledge — and Feser notes the irony that experience supports the causal principle at every turn.

keyTerms.definition: Hume’s argument that because we can conceive of something beginning to exist without a cause, it is possible for something to begin without a cause.
keyTerms.example: Imagining an empty space in which a stone or a coffee cup suddenly appears.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, Book 1, Part 3.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceiving of a thing as having no cause, versus conceiving of it without also conceiving its cause. Feser says Hume achieves only the second — as when we conceive a trilateral without thinking ‘triangle’.

keyTerms.definition: A property that consists in a tendency to produce certain effects under certain conditions.
keyTerms.example: Salt’s solubility; and, as C. B. Martin argues, the tendencies of fundamental particles to affect one another in specific ways.
keyTerms.origin: C. B. Martin and other ‘powers’ theorists; the idea echoes Aristotle’s dynamis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A categorical property, thought of as just ‘being there’ — like shape — with no built-in orientation toward effects.

keyTerms.definition: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted on by an external force.
keyTerms.example: A hockey puck gliding across frictionless ice would keep going indefinitely.
keyTerms.origin: Isaac Newton, Principia (1687), building on Galileo and Descartes.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The claim that motion needs no cause of any kind. At most the law says uniform motion needs no continuously conjoined mover; it says nothing about what keeps the moving body in existence.

keyTerms.definition: Determinism: every event is necessitated by prior conditions plus the laws. Indeterminism: some events are not so necessitated and have only a probability of occurring.
keyTerms.example: On standard quantum mechanics, when a given lead-210 atom decays is indeterministic — yet, as Koons points out, even on the Copenhagen interpretation every transition has causal antecedents: the prior wave state, or that state plus the observation.
keyTerms.origin: ‘Determinism’ became a standard philosophical term in the nineteenth century, though the issue is ancient.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Causation. Feser insists a cause need only make its effect intelligible, not necessary, so indeterministic causation is still causation. That is also why he mentions the de Broglie–Bohm hidden-variable interpretation without relying on it.

keyTerms.definition: Constraints, derived by John Bell, that any theory of local hidden causes must satisfy. Experiments show they are violated: distant measurements are correlated in ways that appear to lack a common cause.
keyTerms.example: Entangled particles measured far apart show correlated results that no local common cause seems able to explain.
keyTerms.origin: Physicist John S. Bell, 1964.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Proof that there is no cause at all. The violations rule out only certain kinds of cause, and several causal readings have been proposed.

keyTerms.definition: The lowest-energy state of a quantum field — not empty nothingness but a physical system with a definite structure and laws, in which particles can briefly appear and disappear.
keyTerms.example: A particle emerging from the ground state of a field: a potential of that field being actualized, not something coming from nothing.
keyTerms.origin: Quantum field theory, twentieth-century physics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Absolute nothingness. The objection ‘particles pop into existence from nothing in the vacuum’ trades on exactly that slide.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas’ idea that some activity follows from a substance’s own nature without a continuously conjoined external mover. Its efficient cause is whatever generated the substance with that nature.
keyTerms.example: A body’s inertial motion, or a lead-210 atom’s tendency to decay, read as flowing from its substantial form.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas; the label ‘spontaneity’ is borrowed from James Weisheipl, Nature and Motion in the Middle Ages.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncaused motion. The motion still has a formal cause in the thing’s nature and an efficient cause in whatever produced the thing.

keyTerms.definition: Arthur Eddington’s contrast between the everyday table — solid, extended, substantial — and the scientific table, a cloud of particles in mostly empty space.
keyTerms.example: An objector uses it to claim that ‘the desk holds up the cup’ is scientifically naïve.
keyTerms.origin: Sir Arthur Eddington, The Nature of the Physical World (1928).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A genuine conflict between physics and common sense. Feser answers that the particles describe the mechanism by which the desk holds the cup — and that nobody raises this against engineers or doctors.

keyTerms.definition: The philosophical view that the natural world studied by science is all there is, with nothing supernatural or immaterial. A holder of the view is a ‘naturalist’.
keyTerms.example: Feser points out that naturalists routinely defend causal theories of knowledge, perception and meaning — which commits them to real causation whatever physics does or does not mention.
keyTerms.origin: A modern philosophical position; Feser calls it the intellectual foundation of much modern atheism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself. Naturalism is a philosophical thesis about what exists, not a scientific finding.

keyTerms.definition: An endless chain in which each step explains the one before only by appealing to something that needs the very same explanation, so that nothing is ever explained. Not every infinite regress is vicious — only the ones that pass the buck.
keyTerms.example: D is actualized by C only insofar as C is actualized by B, and so on without end: the power to actualize is never accounted for. By contrast a beginningless line of fathers begetting sons is harmless, since each begets under his own power.
keyTerms.origin: A classic diagnosis used by Aristotle and Aquinas; ‘passing the explanatory buck’ is Feser’s phrasing.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Any infinite series. Aristotelians allow infinite mathematical series and even beginningless linear causal series; what they rule out is a series of instruments with nothing whose instruments they are.

keyTerms.definition: Mumford and Anjum’s distinction between causation happening within one process and one process merely setting up the conditions for a later, separate process.
keyTerms.example: Sugar dissolving in tea sets up conditions for the tea being drunk ten minutes later; it does not cause the drinking in the way the water and the sugar’s structure cause the dissolving.
keyTerms.origin: Stephen Mumford and Rani Lill Anjum, Getting Causes from Powers (2011).
keyTerms.confuseWith: One long simultaneous chain. This distinction is what stops ‘immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects’ from collapsing all of history into a single instant.

keyTerms.definition: Special relativity’s result that whether two spatially separated events are simultaneous depends on the observer’s frame of reference.
keyTerms.example: Two lightning strikes far apart may be simultaneous in one frame and not in another.
keyTerms.origin: Albert Einstein, special relativity (1905).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The simultaneity of an immediate cause with its effect. Those are parts of one event in one place, not spatially separated events, so the relativistic point does not touch them.

keyTerms.definition: A potential being actualized at the very moment the thing has the feature in question. ‘Concurrent’ means running together in time. Sustaining causes act concurrently with their effects (steps 7–11).
keyTerms.example: The desk actualizes the cup’s being three feet up at the same moment the cup is three feet up; the bonding of the atoms actualizes the water’s existing right now.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s wording in the formal statement of the argument; Latin concurrere, ‘to run together’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine ‘concurrence’ in the technical theological sense — God’s cooperation with creatures’ own actions — which is a separate topic taken up later.

keyTerms.definition: Anything that is actual in some respects and able to be otherwise in others. Every changeable thing is such a mixture; only pure actuality is not.
keyTerms.example: The water is actually water but potentially separate gases; your arm is actually here but potentially there.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–Thomistic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A composite of physical parts. Something could have no physical parts at all and still mix act with potency; the mixture at issue is metaphysical.

keyTerms.definition: The characteristics belonging to God as traditionally conceived. Stage 2 derives ten of them from pure actuality alone: unity, immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality, perfection, goodness, omnipotence, intelligence and omniscience.
keyTerms.example: Steps 15–47 work through them in blocks, each block arguing that the relevant limitation would require an unactualized potential.
keyTerms.origin: Classical philosophical theology (Augustine, Anselm, Avicenna, Maimonides, Aquinas).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Anthropomorphic traits such as a body, a location or moods. These attributes mostly deny limitations rather than adding human features.

keyTerms.definition: A concept that applies to every possible instance of a kind, not just to this or that particular thing. ‘Abstract’ means drawn off from particular instances.
keyTerms.example: Your concept of man applies to every man who exists, has existed or could exist; your concept of triangle covers triangles of every size and shape.
keyTerms.origin: Latin universalis, ‘pertaining to the whole’, and abstractus, ‘drawn away’. Plato and Aristotle.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mental image, which is always particular — a specific size, colour and shape. You cannot picture ‘triangle in general’, but you can understand it.

keyTerms.definition: Refuting a weakened misrepresentation of an opponent’s position instead of the position itself.
keyTerms.example: Attacking ‘everything has a cause’ when the actual premise is ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’. Feser compares the slide to equating ‘all triangles have three sides’ with ‘all figures have three sides’.
keyTerms.origin: An informal fallacy, named for a figure set up only in order to be knocked down.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A fair simplification. Simplifying is fine so long as it keeps the premises the argument actually uses.

keyTerms.definition: Adopted only to rescue a position from an objection, with no independent motivation.
keyTerms.example: The charge that theists narrowed the premise to ‘whatever goes from potential to actual’ just to dodge ‘What caused God?’. Feser answers that the narrower claim is over two thousand years old and follows from Aristotle’s analysis of change.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad hoc, ‘for this (purpose only)’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A principled restriction. A restriction that follows from an independent analysis is not ad hoc, even when it happens to block an objection.

keyTerms.definition: Concluding that something is true because it explains the evidence better than the alternatives do.
keyTerms.example: Feser argues that the principle of causality best explains why we find causes whenever we look, and why elephants and hotels do not appear on front lawns.
keyTerms.origin: The name is Gilbert Harman’s (1965); the pattern is close to what C. S. Peirce called abduction.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Demonstration. The chapter’s main argument is offered as a deductive proof; this kind of inference appears only as extra support against Hume.

keyTerms.definition: Showing that an argument, if it worked, would also establish plainly false conclusions — so something in it must be wrong.
keyTerms.example: Schaffer’s reply to Russell: if absence from the equations showed that causes are unreal, it would equally show that ‘event’, ‘law’ and ‘variable’ are unreal.
keyTerms.origin: A traditional method of refutation, a form of reductio ad absurdum.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Overstating your own conclusion. This is a diagnosis of someone else’s argument, not a complaint about exaggeration.

keyTerms.definition: The broad tradition of thought stemming from Aristotle. It includes scientific theses — geocentrism, the ancient theory of the elements, the natural places toward which bodies were thought to move — many of them refuted, and metaphysical theses such as act and potency, which Feser argues are untouched.
keyTerms.example: That heavy bodies seek the centre of the earth is dead science; that change is the actualization of a potential is metaphysics, which every observation already presupposes.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle (384–322 BC), carried on by his commentators and by the medieval scholastics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotle’s physics in particular. Rejecting his astronomy leaves his metaphysics untouched; running the two together is the whole mistake of the ‘outdated science’ objection.

keyTerms.definition: The part of philosophy that studies the most general features of reality — being, change, causation, substance, act and potency — which any science presupposes.
keyTerms.example: That change is the actualization of a potential is a metaphysical claim: observation and experiment themselves involve going from one experience to another, so no experiment could overturn it.
keyTerms.origin: Greek ta meta ta physika, ‘the (books) after the Physics’, the title given to Aristotle’s treatise.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Metaphysical’ in the bookshop sense of the occult or mystical, or as a synonym for idle speculation.

keyTerms.definition: The traditional conception of God as one, simple, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, omnipotent, omniscient and wholly good — the sustaining cause of everything else.
keyTerms.example: Step 49 identifies the purely actual cause with God so understood, because the attributes derived in Stage 2 are exactly this description.
keyTerms.origin: The mainstream of Jewish, Christian and Islamic philosophical theology: Augustine, Anselm, Avicenna, Maimonides, Aquinas.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism, which pictures God as a very great person alongside the world, changing and in time. The Aristotelian proof supports the classical view instead.

keyTerms.definition: An individual thing that exists in its own right and has features, as opposed to the features themselves. Adjective: ‘substantial’, meaning belonging to a thing as the kind of thing it is.
keyTerms.example: A cup of coffee, a squirrel and a hydrogen atom are substances; being cold, being three feet up and weighing an ounce are features of substances. There is no cooling floating free — only coffee that cools, which is what step 6 insists on.
keyTerms.origin: Latin substantia, ‘standing under’, translating Aristotle’s ousia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Substance’ in the chemist’s sense of a material such as water or copper. In philosophy a substance is a complete individual thing, not a kind of stuff.

keyTerms.definition: What a thing is: the features that make it the kind of thing it is, as opposed to features it merely happens to have. A thing’s nature sets the standard by which it counts as complete or defective.
keyTerms.example: Gathering and storing food belongs to a squirrel’s nature; a scar on its ear does not. That is why the squirrel hit by a car counts as damaged and not merely different.
keyTerms.origin: Latin essentia, coined from esse (‘to be’) to render Aristotle’s phrase for the what-it-is-to-be of a thing.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Essential’ in the loose sense of ‘very important’. Here it means belonging to what the thing is, however unimportant it may seem. (Form is the same reality considered as a pattern an intellect can grasp.)

keyTerms.definition: A thing’s capacity to exist or not to exist at all, as distinct from its capacity to be some particular way. Whatever has such a capacity needs something actualizing it at every moment it exists.
keyTerms.example: The matter now making up the water in your coffee could exist instead as separate hydrogen and oxygen. That it exists as water at this instant is this potential being actualized at this instant — the pivot of step 7.
keyTerms.origin: Feser’s extension, following Aquinas, of Aristotle’s act/potency analysis from change to the sheer existing of things.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The potential to undergo change. The coffee’s potential to grow cold concerns how it is; its potential for existence concerns whether it is there at all.

keyTerms.definition: Simultaneous: cause and effect are parts of one and the same event, however long that event lasts. Instantaneous: happening in a single durationless moment. An immediate cause — the one directly producing the effect — is always simultaneous with its effect and need not be instantaneous.
keyTerms.example: The brick’s pressing into the glass, not the earlier throw, is the immediate cause of the glass giving way. Pushing a chair across a room takes time, yet there is no gap at all between your pushing and its being pushed.
keyTerms.origin: Latin simul, ‘at the same time’, against in instanti, ‘in an instant’. Feser takes the point from W. Norris Clarke and the billiard-ball and brick examples from Mumford and Anjum.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Each other — which is the usual mistake. Asking whether stick and stone move at exactly the same instant misses the point that they are one event.

keyTerms.definition: Something said to be true with no explanation whatsoever — not merely unexplained so far, but unexplainable in principle. Critics often propose that the world’s existence is a brute fact.
keyTerms.example: ‘The water just exists, and that’s that.’ Feser replies that the same matter could have existed as hydrogen and oxygen, so something must account for its existing as water here and now.
keyTerms.origin: A twentieth-century English coinage, made prominent by G.E.M. Anscombe’s ‘On Brute Facts’ and later by debates over the principle of sufficient reason.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A basic or fundamental fact. A fundamental fact may still have an explanation in something deeper; a brute fact is claimed to have none at all.

keyTerms.definition: An argument is valid when the conclusion really does follow from the premises, and sound when it is valid and the premises are also true. Only a sound argument establishes its conclusion. (Premises are the claims offered as starting points; the conclusion is what is supposed to follow.)
keyTerms.example: ‘All cats are green; Tibbles is a cat; so Tibbles is green’ is valid but not sound. Feser insists that to defeat his fifty steps a critic must show that some step is false or that some step does not follow — finding the conclusion strange is not enough.
keyTerms.origin: Standard terminology of modern logic, formalizing distinctions Aristotle drew in the Prior Analytics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everyday ‘valid’ meaning ‘a fair point’. In logic, validity says nothing at all about whether the premises are true.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that aims to establish its conclusion with certainty from premises known to be true, rather than to show it merely likely. Feser offers the five proofs as demonstrations, not as probabilistic hypotheses.
keyTerms.example: The chapter does not argue that God is the likeliest explanation of change. It argues that if change occurs at all, a purely actual actualizer must exist — the way one proves a theorem.
keyTerms.origin: Latin demonstratio, translating Aristotle’s apodeixis, the kind of proof analysed in the Posterior Analytics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inference to the best explanation, which concludes only that something is probably true because it explains the data better than rivals. A demonstration claims more.

keyTerms.definition: Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274) developed Aristotle’s metaphysics into a full philosophical theology; Thomism is the tradition that follows him. Feser’s version of the Aristotelian proof is closest to Aquinas’ First Way, extended from change to existence.
keyTerms.example: The insistence that a hierarchical series needs a first member with underived power, and the idea of God conserving things in being at every moment, come from Aquinas rather than from Aristotle himself.
keyTerms.origin: Named for Thomas of Aquino in Italy. Adjective: ‘Thomistic’ or ‘Thomist’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Aristotelianism generally. All Thomists are Aristotelians of a sort, but Aristotle himself did not hold that God keeps the world in existence moment by moment.

keyTerms.definition: The cosmological model on which the observable universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense early state some fourteen billion years ago. Feser’s argument neither needs it nor is threatened by it.
keyTerms.example: People who hear ‘first cause’ picture God lighting the fuse at the Big Bang. The chapter sets that aside: even a beginningless universe, or a beginningless multiverse of many universes, would still need something holding it in being now.
keyTerms.origin: A nickname coined by Fred Hoyle in a 1949 broadcast; he opposed the theory, and the name stuck anyway.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The first cause of the Aristotelian proof. The Big Bang would be the earliest member of a linear series; this first cause is first in rank, not in time.

keyTerms.definition: Reasoning that invokes God to fill in what science has not yet explained, so that the case for God shrinks as science advances. Feser’s argument is deliberately not of this kind.
keyTerms.example: ‘We can’t explain how life began, so God must have done it.’ The Aristotelian proof instead claims that no possible physics could explain why anything exists at all at this instant, because physics describes how things behave, not what keeps them in being.
keyTerms.origin: The phrase was used critically by the chemist and theologian Charles Coulson, and the idea earlier by Henry Drummond — aimed at believers rather than at atheists.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Any appeal to God in connection with the natural world. The objection bites only when the appeal plugs a temporary hole in science.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only source of genuine knowledge, so that questions science cannot answer are not real questions. It is itself a philosophical claim, not a scientific result.
keyTerms.example: The early Russell’s move from ‘causes do not appear in the equations’ to ‘causation is unreal’ assumes something like scientism — and by that standard ‘event’, ‘law’ and ‘explanation’ would have to go too.
keyTerms.origin: Formed from ‘science’ plus the suffix ‘-ism’; used almost entirely by critics rather than by adherents.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Naturalism, and science itself. Scientism is a claim about the limits of knowledge; naturalism is a claim about what exists.

keyTerms.definition: Any argument that reasons from some general feature of the world — that it changes, that it exists, that it is contingent — to a cause beyond it. The Aristotelian proof is one member of this family.
keyTerms.example: The kalām argument (from medieval Islamic theology, defended today by William Lane Craig) reasons from the world’s having a beginning; the Aristotelian proof grants a possibly beginningless world and reasons from what sustains things now.
keyTerms.origin: Greek kosmos, ‘world’ or ‘ordered whole’; the label was popularized by Kant, who grouped such arguments together in order to criticize them.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The design argument, which reasons from apparent purpose or fine-tuning in nature. Cosmological arguments do not depend on how orderly the world looks.

keyTerms.definition: The attempt to establish truths about God by reasoning from the world, without appealing to scripture, revelation or religious authority. This book is an exercise in natural theology.
keyTerms.example: None of the fifty steps appeals to a sacred text; the chapter answers Hume, Russell and Newton rather than quoting anyone’s scriptures.
keyTerms.origin: Latin theologia naturalis, contrasted since the Middle Ages with theologia revelata, revealed theology.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Revealed theology, which starts from what a religious tradition claims God has disclosed.

keyTerms.definition: A feature a substance has without its being the kind of thing it is — colour, temperature, size, location. Adjective: ‘accidental’, used more generally for any feature a thing merely happens to have rather than has essentially.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s growing cold is an accidental change: the coffee is still coffee. The fly’s dying is a substantial change: the fly stops being a fly. Being under seven feet tall is likewise accidental to being president.
keyTerms.origin: Latin accidens, ‘what befalls’, translating Aristotle’s symbebēkos.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Accident’ meaning a mishap; and the fallacy of accident, which is the mistake of treating an accidental feature as if it were essential.

keyTerms.definition: Immanuel Kant’s worry that principles like causality are learned from experience and so cannot legitimately be applied beyond the world of experience, to something unobservable.
keyTerms.example: Fine, air conditioners cool rooms and we watch it happen — but you cannot ride that principle out past space and time to an immaterial actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason (1781), which restricted the categories of the understanding to possible experience.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hume’s objection, which denies that the causal principle is necessary at all. Kant grants it inside experience and doubts only its reach — and Feser answers that its ground, that a potential cannot actualize itself, is completely general, just as Euclid’s geometry is not confined to figures drawn in black ink.

keyTerms.definition: Bertrand Russell’s claim that causation is a relic of a bygone age, because the equations of physics describe relations between events without mentioning causes.
keyTerms.example: Russell wrote that in the motions of mutually gravitating bodies there is no cause and no effect, merely a formula. Feser replies that the same reasoning would eliminate events, laws and explanation as well.
keyTerms.origin: Bertrand Russell, ‘On the Notion of Cause’ (1912).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hume’s scepticism about causation, which concerns what we can know or conceive. Russell’s is a claim about what physics implies — and the later Russell himself granted that physics leaves the intrinsic character of events unknown.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which an unstable nucleus emits particles and becomes a different nucleus, at a time that quantum theory predicts only probabilistically. It is the standard example offered against the principle of causality.
keyTerms.example: Nothing seems to make this lead-210 atom decay at this particular moment. Feser’s reply: its nature grounds the probability (formal cause), something generated it, and something keeps it in existence now (efficient causes).
keyTerms.origin: Discovered by Henri Becquerel and the Curies in the 1890s; the probabilistic account comes from quantum mechanics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An uncaused event. Undetermined is not the same as uncaused: a cause can have a genuine tendency to produce an effect without fixing exactly when.

distinctions.name: Per accidens vs. per se causal series

left.label: Per accidens (linear, accidentally ordered)
left.desc: Members are strung out in time and each has its own causal power relative to the others; a later member can keep acting after earlier ones disappear (the air conditioner runs after you leave; Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive). Such a series could in principle have no beginning.

right.label: Per se (hierarchical, essentially ordered)
right.desc: Every member but the first has only derived, instrumental power and acts only while being acted on (desk held by floor held by foundation). Remove the source and the whole series stops at once. It must have a first member with underived power — even if it were infinitely long.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is the hinge of the entire proof. The argument concedes an infinite past and rests everything on the per se series that sustains things in being right now. Most popular objections (‘the universe might be eternal’, ‘why can’t the chain go back forever?’) confuse the two.

distinctions.name: Actuality vs. potentiality

left.label: Actuality
left.desc: What a thing actually is here and now; only the actual can act or cause.

right.label: Potentiality
right.desc: What a thing can become — real but unrealized, determinate (coffee can cool, not turn into soup), and incapable of actualizing itself.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It explains change without Parmenides’ something-from-nothing, grounds the principle of causality, and defines the conclusion (pure actuality) from which every divine attribute is derived.

distinctions.name: ‘First’ in time vs. ‘first’ in the order of dependence

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest member of a series, the one at the beginning — e.g., whatever triggered the Big Bang.

right.label: First as primary / underived
right.desc: The member whose causal power is built in rather than borrowed, and on which all the others depend right now for their power to act.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument’s First Cause is first in the second sense. That is why the age of the universe, and whether time had a beginning, are irrelevant.

distinctions.name: Cause of coming-to-be vs. cause of being (sustaining cause)

left.label: Cause of becoming
left.desc: What originally produced a thing — the brewing of the coffee, the chemical reaction that bonded hydrogen and oxygen, the parents who begot a child.

right.label: Cause of being
right.desc: What makes the thing exist right now, at this instant — what actualizes the matter’s potential to be water rather than separate gases here and now.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument asks the second question. Answers to the first (‘a past process made it’) or about possible destruction (‘nothing has broken it up yet’) don’t touch it.

distinctions.name: ‘Everything has a cause’ vs. ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’

left.label: The straw man
left.desc: Everything whatsoever has a cause — which would indeed make ‘What caused God?’ a fair question.

right.label: The actual principle
right.desc: Only what passes from potency to act needs an actualizer; what is purely actual has nothing to be actualized, so it neither needs nor could have a cause.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Keeping them apart defuses the most common objection to every first-cause argument. The difference is like that between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all figures have three sides’.

distinctions.name: Formal vs. virtual vs. eminent possession of an effect

left.label: Formally
left.desc: The cause has the very feature it gives (I hand you a twenty from my wallet).

right.label: Virtually or eminently
right.desc: The cause has the power to obtain it (bank credit) or the higher power to produce such things at all (authority to print money).

distinctions.whyItMatters: Proportionate causality does not mean God must be a cat to cause cats. The forms of things are in God eminently — as ideas in an intellect — which is how Stage 2 derives intelligence and omniscience.

distinctions.name: Absence from the representation vs. representation of absence
