left.label: Absent from the representation
left.desc: A black-and-white drawing contains no color; mathematical physics contains no ‘causes’, only equations.

right.label: Represented as absent
right.desc: A claim that the scene itself is colorless, or that nature itself lacks causation.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Russell’s, Newtonian, relativistic and quantum objections all slide from the first to the second. If a method is guaranteed to leave something out, its omission is no evidence the thing is missing.

distinctions.name: Unmoved vs. unmovable

left.label: Unmoved (in fact)
left.desc: A first actualizer that isn’t actually being actualized while it acts, but might still have unrealized potentials.

right.label: Unmovable (purely actual)
right.desc: An actualizer with no potentiality at all, and so incapable of being actualized.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only the second yields the divine attributes. Feser argues the first is incoherent as a first actualizer of existence: any potential in it would need an actualizer, sending us beyond it or into a vicious regress.

illustrations.title: The cooling cup of coffee
illustrations.body:
Hot coffee on your desk has a real potential to become cold — along with potentials to stain the rug or wake you up — but no potential to become chicken soup or a live chicken. When it cools, that potential is actualized, not by itself (a mere potential can’t do anything) but by the actual coolness of the air or by ice cubes you drop in.

Use it to teach three things at once: change is real, potentiality is something rather than nothing (answering Parmenides), and potentials need actual actualizers (the principle of causality).

illustrations.title: The cup on the desk on the floor on the earth — and the hanging lamp
illustrations.body:
The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *right now*; the desk holds it only because the floor holds the desk *right now*; and so on to the foundation and the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture, held by the ceiling, held by walls and foundation. Knock out any lower member and everything above it falls at once.

This is Feser’s model of a **hierarchical** series: every intermediate member is like an instrument with borrowed power. Contrast the air conditioner, which keeps cooling the room after you’ve left the house (a **linear** series).

illustrations.title: The painter, the brush — and the infinitely long handle
illustrations.body:
The painter paints the picture; the brush is merely his instrument. A brush has no power to move itself, and it wouldn’t gain any if its handle were infinitely long. If the brush is moving, something with built-in power to move it must be at work.

This shows why ‘first cause’ doesn’t mean ‘earliest cause’, and why making a hierarchical series infinite doesn’t remove the need for a primary cause: more instruments are still just instruments.

illustrations.title: What keeps the water in the coffee existing?
illustrations.body:
The matter that is now water could exist instead as separate hydrogen and oxygen. What actualizes its potential to be water *at this instant*? ‘A reaction in the past’ tells you how it got here; ‘nothing has split it yet’ tells you how it might stop existing. Chemical bonding just restates the question, and atomic structure pushes it one level down to subatomic particles.

We have a hierarchical series of actualizers of *existence*, which must end in something whose existence needs no actualizing — pure actuality.

illustrations.title: The $20 gift
illustrations.body:
I can give you $20 only if I somehow have it: a twenty in my wallet (formally), money in my bank account (virtually), or even the power to print twenty-dollar bills (eminently). If I have it in none of these ways, I can’t give it.

This illustrates the principle of proportionate causality, which Stage 2 uses to show that the cause of all things must contain their forms — not by *being* a cat or a tree, but eminently, as ideas in an intellect.

illustrations.title: Metal detectors, easy courses, and the drunk under the streetlamp
illustrations.body:
A metal detector’s success doesn’t show there’s no wood or stone in the ground. A student who takes only classes he knows he’ll ace can’t conclude other subjects contain nothing important. A drunk who finds things under the streetlamp can’t infer his keys aren’t somewhere in the dark.

Physics deliberately attends only to what can be mathematized, so its silence about causes, potentials, or intrinsic natures is no evidence against them. Feser uses these analogies against Russell, and again against the inertia and quantum objections.

illustrations.title: The black-and-white drawing and the ‘color hold’
illustrations.body:
A line drawing has no color, but that doesn’t show the scene was colorless — the method just can’t record color. In a ‘color hold’, some contours are left out of the ink and supplied only by the color added later; a sharp viewer can still infer, from the lines that are drawn, where the missing edges of a cube must be.

Physics is the line art; physics plus metaphysics is the finished colored picture. Quantum theory, with what Heisenberg compared to Aristotle’s *potentia*, may be line art whose lines hint at the causality they don’t depict.

illustrations.title: Mirrors all the way down
illustrations.body:
A mirror shows the image of a face that is in another mirror, which shows the image in another, and so on without end. Even if such an infinite hall of mirrors were possible, the image must come from an actual face that isn’t just reflecting something else. You can’t have mirror images with no face.

In the same way, an infinite hierarchy of instrumental causes would still need a source of underived causal power outside the series.

illustrations.title: The movie on the screen
illustrations.body:
The image on a cinema screen exists only as long as the projector is running and its bulb is shining. It doesn’t matter how long the film has been playing or whether it had a ‘first frame’; at every instant, the picture exists only because light is being cast on it *now*. Switch off the bulb and the picture doesn’t fade out over centuries — it vanishes instantly.

This is a good way to convey a per se series of existence: the question is not ‘what started the movie?’ but ‘what is keeping the picture there right now?’ (Where the analogy breaks down: the bulb itself needs power; only something purely actual would be a source that needs no source.)

illustrations.title: A train of boxcars with no engine
illustrations.body:
Each boxcar is pulled by the one in front of it. Add more boxcars — a thousand, a million, infinitely many — and you still have no motion at all unless there is an engine, something that pulls without being pulled. Length doesn’t turn borrowed motion into motion that nobody supplies.

This helps skeptics see why ‘just make the regress infinite’ doesn’t work for instrumental causes. Stress that the engine is ‘first’ by *nature* (it pulls on its own power), not merely by position at the front.

objections.title: A first cause isn’t the God of theism
objections.whoRaises: Typical skeptic; many popular critics of cosmological arguments
objections.objection: Even if the argument gets you to some first cause, it can’t tell you what that cause is like. For all it shows, the cause could be an impersonal force, a quantum field, or a committee of gods. Calling it ‘God’ is a bait-and-switch.
objections.reply:
Feser calls this objection common but entirely ungrounded. The Aristotelian argument doesn’t reach a vague ‘something’; it reaches something **purely actual**, and pure actuality has consequences:

1. No potential means no change: **immutable**.
2. No change means no time: **eternal**.
3. No change or time means no matter: **immaterial, incorporeal**.
4. No unrealized potential means no privation: **perfect** and **fully good**.
5. Nothing to differentiate two such beings: **one**.
6. The source of all actualizing power: **omnipotent**.
7. By proportionate causality, the forms of everything must be in it abstractly: **intelligent** and **omniscient**.

That is the traditional concept of God, and it is derived, not assumed. A fuller defense of each attribute comes in the later chapter on the divine nature.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘those derivations rest on contested assumptions’, agree that they need defending — Feser says so himself — but point out that the objection has now changed. It is no longer ‘a first-cause argument *can’t* tell you anything about the cause’; it’s ‘I dispute step 16 (or 28, or 42)’. That is a specific premise you can examine together. Also note that an impersonal force or quantum field has potentials (it can be in different states), so it can’t be what is purely actual.

objections.title: The universe may not have had a beginning
objections.whoRaises: Readers who assume every theistic argument is a ‘Big Bang’ argument; defenders of eternal or cyclic cosmologies
objections.objection: The argument says that if you trace causes back in time you reach God at the beginning of the universe. But we don’t know the universe had a beginning — the Big Bang might have come from an earlier universe, and an infinite multiverse might have no start at all.
objections.reply: This is a misreading. Feser explicitly **grants**, for argument’s sake, that the universe — or a series of universes — might stretch infinitely into the past. Aristotle himself believed the world was eternal. Whether the cosmos had a beginning is **irrelevant** because the argument concerns a **hierarchical** series of causes that sustain things **here and now**, not a linear series running back through time. Even in a beginningless universe, the water in your coffee exists at this moment only because its potential to exist as water is being actualized at this moment.
objections.pushback: If they still insist ‘but the chain has to go back to God at some point’, draw two diagrams: a horizontal line of events (linear — can be infinite) and a vertical stack of dependencies at a single moment (hierarchical — needs a top). Ask them which one the argument uses. Beginningless-multiverse cosmologies speak only to the horizontal line.

objections.title: Fallacy of composition: the whole universe needn’t have a cause
objections.whoRaises: Hume- and Russell-style critics; introductory philosophy textbooks (Feser names no one for this objection in the chapter)
objections.objection: Even if every part of the universe has a cause, it doesn’t follow that the universe as a whole has one. Inferring a cause of the whole from causes of the parts is a fallacy of composition.
objections.reply: No premise of the argument is about the universe as a whole. It begins with **any single object existing now** — a stone, a cup of coffee — and shows that for *that one thing* to exist even for a moment, a purely actual cause must be actualizing it at that moment. Feser does go on to say this applies to every material thing, and so to the universe as a whole — but that is a **consequence** drawn from the argument, not a premise it relies on.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘generalizing from the coffee to everything is still composition’, point out that it’s not composition but ordinary universal instantiation: the reasoning applies to *each* thing with a potential for existence, one at a time, because each has that potential. No claim about the whole is inferred from the parts.

objections.title: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
objections.whoRaises: Popular atheist writers; the most common objection in casual conversation
objections.objection: The argument says everything needs a cause, then exempts God. If God can exist uncaused, why not the universe? This is special pleading.
objections.reply:
Two points.

1. The argument never says ‘everything has a cause’. Its principle is that **whatever goes from potential to actual** needs an actualizer.
2. The exemption is not arbitrary; it follows from the principle’s own rationale. Things need causes *because* they have potentials that must be actualized. What is **purely actual** has no potentials — nothing in it that needs to be, or even could be, actualized. So it is the one thing that neither needs nor could have a cause.

The universe, by contrast, is full of potentiality — it changes constantly — so it is exactly the sort of thing that needs an actualizer.
objections.pushback: If they reply ‘there’s no real difference between those two principles’, give Feser’s analogy: that’s like saying there’s no real difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all geometrical figures have three sides’. The first is restricted to a kind, for a reason; the second isn’t.

objections.title: ‘The potential-to-actual formulation is an ad hoc dodge’
objections.whoRaises: Critics trying to rescue the ‘What caused God?’ objection
objections.objection: Theists only avoid saying ‘everything has a cause’ because they know it invites ‘What caused God?’. The careful formulation was invented to escape the objection.
objections.reply:
Feser identifies three problems.

1. **Ad hominem.** Even if the motive were suspect, that wouldn’t show the principle is false or the argument unsound. Motives don’t refute arguments.
2. **Historically false.** For over twenty-three centuries — Aristotle, Aquinas, and their successors to today — defenders of the argument have *always* stated it this way. It wasn’t cooked up to answer modern critics.
3. **Not ad hoc at all.** The principle falls straight out of Aristotle’s analysis of change, independent of any argument for God. You don’t need to believe in God to find it implausible that a mere potential could actualize itself.

If anything is ad hoc, it is the attempt to save an objection aimed at a straw man.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘fine, but it still conveniently lets God off the hook’, ask them to state a principle that would require a purely actual being to have a cause. They will have to show that pure actuality has some potential needing actualization — which contradicts what ‘purely actual’ means.

objections.title: Hume: we can conceive of something popping into existence uncaused
objections.whoRaises: David Hume and empiricists following him
objections.objection: I can imagine an empty space in which a stone suddenly appears with nothing causing it. Whatever is conceivable is possible, so an uncaused beginning is possible — and then perhaps something can go from potential to actual with no actualizer.
objections.reply:
Feser gives three replies.

1. **Imagining without a cause isn’t imagining no cause.** Picturing the stone appearing is only conceiving of it *without also conceiving of* its cause. You can think of a trilateral without thinking of it as a triangle, or of a man without thinking of his height — but no trilateral fails to be a triangle and no man lacks a height. Conceiving A without B is not conceiving A existing without B.
2. **Anscombe’s point.** What makes the scenario one of *coming into existence* rather than the stone’s being *transported* from somewhere? The only difference lies in the kind of cause involved (being made versus being moved). So spelling out the scenario brings causation back in.
3. **Experience strongly supports the principle.** We find causes when we look; when we don’t (an unsolved murder) we reasonably assume they are there. If the principle were false, nothing would be needed to produce anything — as W. Norris Clarke says, elephants and hotels could appear on your lawn, and should do so constantly. They don’t. The best explanation is that potentiality by its nature requires actualization.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe the regularity is just a brute fact’, point out that it would then be a colossal, unexplained coincidence that the world behaves exactly as it would if the principle were true. An empiricist of all people should follow the evidence, and the evidence overwhelmingly favors the principle.

objections.title: Kant: causality applies only within experience
objections.whoRaises: Immanuel Kant and Kantian critics
objections.objection: We learn about causation from the empirical world. Even if the principle holds there, what entitles us to extend it beyond all possible experience to something immaterial, timeless and unobservable?
objections.reply: We do learn the principle from experience, but that doesn’t limit its scope. We conclude that the things we experience need causes not **because we experience them** but **because they are merely potential until made actual**. The principle that no potential actualizes itself is fully general, so it applies wherever there is potentiality, observable or not. Feser’s analogy: we learn Euclidean geometry from diagrams, usually in black ink, but its theorems apply to figures of any color or none. Restricting causality to what we can experience is like restricting geometry to figures we can see.
objections.pushback: If they press the full Kantian view that causality is just a category our minds impose, note that the argument can start from change in our own experience — which even a Kantian grants — and that the Kantian theory itself makes sweeping claims about how minds and appearances are related (causal-sounding claims) that go beyond experience. More in the later chapter on objections.

objections.title: Russell: physics has no place for causes
objections.whoRaises: Bertrand Russell (‘On the Notion of Cause’, 1912) and eliminativists about causation
objections.objection: Mature physics describes the world with differential equations relating events. Nowhere in the equations is there a ‘cause’ — just a formula. Causation is a pre-scientific relic.
objections.reply:
Feser gives four replies.

1. **It proves too much.** ‘Event’, ‘law’ and ‘explanation’ don’t appear in the equations either, yet science can’t do without them. As Jonathan Schaffer puts it, this is like saying mathematics has eliminated the variable because the word ‘variable’ is never written in the equations.
2. **Physics does use causal notions.** C. B. Martin notes that fundamental particles have dispositions — tendencies to produce effects when they interact in certain ways.
3. **Other sciences clearly use causation**, and they aren’t reducible to physics — biology, the social sciences, arguably chemistry. And naturalists themselves defend causal theories of knowledge, perception and meaning.
4. **Physics isn’t exhaustive.** It captures only the mathematically describable structure of things; the later Russell admitted it says nothing about the intrinsic nature of what changes. Inferring that nothing lies beyond its reach is like concluding there’s no wood because your metal detector didn’t beep.

Moreover, something must make the world actually follow these equations, and if what the equations describe is real change, that change is actualization of potential — causation.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘fine, causation is only in our experience, not in reality’, reply that then causation is at least in our experience — one experience actualizing the next, as when setting up an experiment is followed by observing the result — and that is enough actualization of potential to start the argument. And our knowledge of physics depends on the world causally affecting our senses.

objections.title: Newton’s law of inertia: motion continues without a cause
objections.whoRaises: Critics of Aristotle’s ‘whatever is moved is moved by another’; many philosophers of physics
objections.objection: Newton’s first law says a body in uniform motion keeps moving with no force acting on it. So change (continued motion) happens without any cause, and the principle of causality is false.
objections.reply:
Three responses.

1. **Different question.** Inertia concerns events in time — how molecules move through a cup. The argument is about what actualizes a thing’s **existence** at a moment — what makes these components constitute a water molecule right now. Newton’s law presupposes such things; it can’t explain their existence.
2. **Laws presuppose natures.** A law of nature is shorthand for how things with a certain nature tend to behave. What makes it the case that there are things with *this* nature, following *this* law rather than another? What actualizes that? Mechanics can’t say.
3. **Mathematical abstraction.** As James Weisheipl argues, mathematical physics doesn’t prove inertia; it *assumes* it. To write equations, it treats uniform motion as a baseline needing no explanation and quantifies only *changes* in motion. Newton set aside physical causes and sought quantities that could be equated. So such physics can neither affirm nor deny causal realities.

Inertia therefore doesn’t refute the principle of causality — it *couldn’t*. However inertia is interpreted, it must be made compatible with the principle, which reaches deeper than physics.
objections.pushback: If they ask what the Aristotelian does say about inertial motion, mention Feser’s footnote: following Aquinas’ idea of motions that follow ‘spontaneously’ from a thing’s nature, some contemporary Aristotelians treat inertia as the way a body tends to move given its form. The efficient cause is what generated the body with that nature — and ultimately what sustains it in being. So inertial motion isn’t uncaused; it just doesn’t need a continuously pushing external mover.

objections.title: Einstein’s block universe: change is an illusion
objections.whoRaises: Eternalist interpreters of relativity (following Minkowski); some physicists and philosophers of time
objections.objection: On the four-dimensional block universe, past, present and future are all equally real, like places on a map. Nothing ever passes from potential to actual; the flow of time is just how consciousness represents things. So the argument’s first premise fails.
objections.reply:
Feser notes that the block interpretation is controversial even among physicists (he points to Lee Smolin), but he doesn’t need to settle it.

1. **Self-undermining.** Relativity rests on observation and experiment — making predictions and then testing them, going from ignorance to knowledge. All that is change. So denying change entirely undercuts the evidence for the theory itself (a point made by Richard Healey). At most one could say change exists only in the mind, and change in the mind is still actualization of potential.
2. **Existence still needs an actualizer.** Even if nothing changed anywhere, a thing’s very existence involves actualized potential. The block universe as a whole — this block rather than some other, or none — would still need an actualizer distinct from it.

Relativity at most affects **how** we apply the principle of causality, not **whether** we must.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘change in the mind is also an illusion’, point out that an illusion is itself a mental event that comes and goes, and that coming to believe the block theory is a change of mind. Denying all change is not a position anyone can coherently hold — any more than Parmenides could.

objections.title: Quantum indeterminism means some events have no cause
objections.whoRaises: Popular science writers; some physicists
objections.objection: Quantum events are fundamentally probabilistic. Nothing determines when a particular atom decays or where an electron is detected. So there are changes without causes.
objections.reply:
Some point out that de Broglie–Bohm’s hidden-variable interpretation makes quantum mechanics deterministic after all. But the deeper point is that **causation doesn’t require determinism**. A cause must make its effect *intelligible*, not *necessary*. Even on the indeterministic Copenhagen interpretation, as Robert Koons notes, every transition has causal antecedents — the prior wave state, or the prior state plus the measurement.

And more fundamentally: mathematical physics abstracts from causal and qualitative content. That a theory assigns no deterministic cause doesn’t show there is no cause; **absence from the representation isn’t a representation of absence**.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘then your “cause” is doing no work’, notice that the argument does not actually need the decay’s *timing* to be caused. Even a genuinely uncaused quantum transition would be a transition *in* something — an atom, a field — and that something exists at that instant only because its potential to exist as that kind of thing is being actualized. The argument runs on existence at a moment, not on predictability.

objections.title: The Bell inequalities show uncaused correlations
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers of physics; popularizers of quantum entanglement
objections.objection: Experiments confirming violations of the Bell inequalities show correlations between distant measurements that can’t be explained by any common cause or by signals traveling at or below light speed. So there are correlations with no causal explanation.
objections.reply:
Feser notes several proposals that preserve causality: allowing causal influences faster than light, backward causation, an absolute reference frame, or a law according to which the correlations hold (options discussed by Koons and Alexander Pruss). All raise questions, as does every interpretation of quantum mechanics.

But the decisive point is methodological. Quantum theory is a mathematical representation that by its nature leaves causal content out. That it doesn’t *show* a cause is no evidence there isn’t one — just as a black-and-white drawing is no evidence that the scene lacks color. And the entangled systems themselves exist and have their natures only because their potentials are being actualized.
objections.pushback: If they say you’re just ‘hiding behind metaphysics’, note that the burden runs the other way: the objection claims physics proves something (no cause) that physics’ method is incapable of detecting either way. Feser’s point is that such objections aren’t even well-formulated.

objections.title: Virtual particles pop into existence from nothing
objections.whoRaises: Popular cosmology (e.g. claims that a ‘universe from nothing’ is possible)
objections.objection: Quantum field theory says particles come into and go out of existence at random in the vacuum. That is something coming into being with no cause.
objections.reply: Pruss suggests either a hidden-variable account or treating the system described by quantum field theory as the indeterministic cause of these events. More importantly, a quantum vacuum isn’t *nothing*: it is a physical system with a definite structure, governed by laws, and bursting with potentialities. Particles emerging from it are **potentials of the field being actualized** — exactly what the principle of causality addresses, not a counterexample to it. And the field itself exists here and now with that nature only because its potential for existence is being actualized.
objections.pushback: If they insist the events are random, return to the point that randomness isn’t causelessness (indeterministic causation) and that laws describe the behavior of things with natures — so the question becomes: what actualizes the existence of a field with *this* nature?

objections.title: Radioactive decay is uncaused
objections.whoRaises: Philosophers of science; popular critics
objections.objection: A lead-210 atom may decay into mercury-206 with no outside interference, at a time nothing determines. Only a probability can be assigned. So the decay has no cause.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘calling it the atom’s nature is just a label’, reply that it is exactly what physicists appeal to: lead-210 has this half-life *because* it is lead-210 and not some other isotope. That is grounding in the kind of thing it is — which is what a formal cause is.

objections.title: Aristotelianism was refuted by modern science
objections.whoRaises: Popular histories of the Scientific Revolution; many scientists
objections.objection: Modern science overthrew Aristotle. An Aristotelian argument for God is as obsolete as Aristotelian astronomy.
objections.reply: Feser calls this sloppy: it lumps together very different ideas. ‘Aristotelianism’ labels a huge body of scientific, philosophical, theological and political claims. Some specifically **scientific** ones — geocentrism, the four elements, natural places — really were refuted. But the claim that change is actualization of potential is **metaphysical**, and science hasn’t refuted it. On the contrary, science presupposes change (observation and experiment involve moving from one experience to another), so every possible scientific theory presupposes the actualization of potential. The book’s arguments rest on these deeper metaphysical foundations, not on revisable scientific claims.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘metaphysics has been replaced by science’, ask what scientific experiment could establish that only science yields knowledge. That claim is itself philosophical — and a later chapter shows science rests on metaphysical foundations it cannot justify on its own.

objections.title: Eddington’s two tables: the examples are scientifically naïve
objections.whoRaises: Readers of Arthur Eddington’s The Nature of the Physical World; scientistic critics
objections.objection: Physics shows a desk is really a cloud of particles in mostly empty space; cups ‘rest’ on it only because particles keep colliding. So talk of a desk holding up a cup, a floor holding up a desk, etc., gets the science wrong, and an argument built on such examples is poorly grounded.
objections.reply:
Feser thinks this sounds sophisticated but is silly, for three reasons.

1. **No competition.** It assumes common sense and physics compete. That the floor, desk and cup are made of colliding particles doesn’t mean the floor doesn’t really hold up the desk; physics just describes the **mechanism** by which it does.
2. **Selective.** No one accuses an engineer (how thick a foundation must be to support a building) or a doctor (how a herniated disk fails to support the spine) of outdated science for ignoring particle physics.
3. **Irrelevant.** The examples were only meant to introduce actualization of potential and the linear/hierarchical distinction. Those concepts apply whether we speak of desks or particle clouds. The details affect **how**, not **whether**, we apply them. We don’t object to a physicist’s thought experiment about riding a light beam that photons are too small to sit on.
objections.pushback: If they still worry, restate the example at the particle level: the cup’s particles are held at a certain height by electromagnetic interactions with the desk’s particles, which depend on the floor’s, and so on — still a hierarchical series of actualizers, just described more finely. And the deeper series (of existence) runs from molecules to atoms to subatomic particles anyway.

objections.title: There are no truly simultaneous causes
objections.whoRaises: Humean critics; physics-minded skeptics
objections.objection: Hierarchical series rely on causes acting simultaneously with their effects. But precise measurement would show a time lag between stick and stone, desk and cup. And if immediate causes were simultaneous, every causal chain would collapse into one instant. Besides, relativity makes simultaneity observer-relative.
objections.reply:
Feser answers point by point.

1. **Simultaneous isn’t instantaneous.** Pushing a stone takes time, but the stick’s moving it and its being moved are one event. Clarke: it takes time to push a chair across a room, but there is no time between the pushing and the chair’s being pushed.
2. **Immediate causes are simultaneous with effects.** Following Mumford and Anjum: it isn’t ball A’s earlier motion that strictly causes B’s, but A’s impact on B, which is one event with B’s being impacted. It isn’t the throw that immediately breaks the glass but the brick pressing into it.
3. **No collapse.** Distinguish causation *within* one process from one process setting up conditions for another. Sugar dissolving in tea, the tea being drunk, the tea being digested: each is a causal process, but the dissolving doesn’t cause the drinking in the same sense; it just sets the stage.
4. **Relativity is irrelevant.** Relativity of simultaneity concerns distinct, spatially separated events; here cause and effect are parts of the same event at the same place.
5. **Not the point anyway.** What makes a series hierarchical is derivative, instrumental power, not simultaneity. And the argument’s key series concerns a thing’s existence at an instant — which raises no issue of duration at all.
objections.pushback: If they keep pressing on timing, grant it and move to point 5: ‘Forget stones and sticks. At this instant, the water exists as water rather than as separate hydrogen and oxygen. What actualizes that?’ The question arises at any instant, however events are timed.

objections.title: Infinite series are possible, so why not an infinite hierarchical regress?
objections.whoRaises: Graham Oppy (Arguing about Gods) and others who say no reason is given to rule out infinite regress
objections.objection: Mathematics is full of infinite series — the natural numbers go on forever without a first. Aquinas and Feser give no real reason why a causal series couldn’t do the same.
objections.reply: Oppy ignores the crucial role of **instrumental** causation. Mathematical series involve no instrumental and primary causes — indeed no causation at all — so they’re not relevant counterexamples. Aristotelians don’t reject infinite series as such: they allow infinite mathematical series and even beginningless *linear* causal series. What they deny is a hierarchical series with no source of underived power. In such a series every member acts only by power received; if nothing has the power unreceived, nothing acts at all. An infinitely long brush handle still can’t move itself; an infinite hall of mirrors still needs a real face. Without a first cause we just pass the explanatory buck forever.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘each member is explained by the previous one, so every member is explained’, reply that in a per se series, no member explains the *power* it passes along — it only transmits what it receives. Explaining each transmission by another transmission never explains where the power comes from, just as adding more boxcars never explains how the train moves.

objections.title: Calling causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question
objections.whoRaises: Jordan Howard Sobel (Logic and Theism)
objections.objection: To call the intermediate causes ‘instruments’ already assumes there is some first cause using them. We have no reason to think things depend on hierarchical series of that kind unless we already accept theism.
objections.reply: No question is begged. Calling something an instrumental cause means only that it **derives its causal power from something else**. That description doesn’t itself say that a series of such causes can’t go to infinity, or that some cause has underived power — those are conclusions argued for separately. Even a skeptic understands that a stick can’t move a stone under its own power, whatever he goes on to say about whether a regress of moved movers must end.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘but why believe ordinary things depend on hierarchical series at all?’, go back to the water: its matter could be separate gases, so its being water now is an actualized potential; bonding and atomic structure just push the question down a level. That dependence is shown by analyzing ordinary cases, not by presupposing God.

objections.title: Unmoved isn’t unmovable: the first mover might have unrealized potentials
objections.whoRaises: Sophisticated critics of the attribute derivations
objections.objection: Grant a first actualizer that isn’t being actualized while it acts. Why must it be *purely* actual? It could have potentials that are actualized at other times, or never. Then it wouldn’t be one, eternal, immaterial or perfect.
objections.reply:
The regress that matters is of actualizers of **existence**. The first actualizer is first because it actualizes others’ existence without its own existence needing to be actualized. Suppose it had a potential that must be actualized for it to exist. What actualizes it?

- **Something else?** Then it isn’t the first actualizer after all.
- **A purely actual part of itself?** Then *that part* is the real first actualizer, and the potential ‘part’ is just its first effect.
- **A part mixing act and potency?** Then what actualizes *that part’s* potentials? Another mixed part — a vicious regress.

So there is no coherent first actualizer of existence that isn’t purely actual. To admit a first actualizer at all is to admit pure actuality, with all the attributes that follow from it.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe its extra potentials have nothing to do with its existence — they’re just unused capacities’, reply that any unrealized potential makes a thing a composite of act and potency, and a composite exists only if something makes that combination actual. For the supposed first actualizer, that ‘something’ must be either another being or a part of itself — which lands you straight back in the three-way dilemma. (The Neo-Platonic and Thomistic chapters, and the chapter on the divine attributes, develop this further.)

objections.title: A purely actual actualizer is incoherent — to cause is to change
objections.whoRaises: Critics who argue causation always involves the cause’s own change
objections.objection: Anything that actualizes another thing must itself undergo change in doing so, so it must have potentials being actualized. A cause that acts without changing is a contradiction.
objections.reply:
Three responses.

1. **It begs the question.** The argument claims to prove no potential could be actualized without a purely actual actualizer. If the premises are true and the logic valid, the conclusion is true and so coherent. The critic must find a false premise or bad inference, not just assert the conclusion is impossible. Otherwise the argument shows a purely actual actualizer is possible, since actual.
2. **Fallacy of accident.** Observed causes change when they act — your arm moves to move the stick. But that’s a contingent feature of the causes we meet, not an essential feature of causing. Compare: every U.S. president so far has been under seven feet tall, but it doesn’t follow no one taller *could* be president.
3. **No contradiction.** An ‘immortal mortal’ is contradictory; a ‘purely actual actualizer’ is simply something that actualizes without being actualized. And we can say *why* our causes must change: they are **limited** — an arm is actually here and only potentially there, so to get the stick there its own potential must be actualized. Pure act has no such limits.
objections.pushback: If they ask ‘but how can something act without changing?’, compare it to the way a truth ‘makes’ a conclusion follow without anything happening to it, or the way an attractive object draws you without itself moving (Aristotle’s own image). These are imperfect analogies, but they show that ‘acting’ and ‘undergoing change’ are not the same concept.

objections.title: Why not let the universe, energy, or the laws of physics be the purely actual thing?
objections.whoRaises: Modern naturalists (a common response, not discussed by name in the chapter)
objections.objection: Fine — something has to be at the bottom of the hierarchy. Why not the universe itself, or conserved mass-energy, or the fundamental laws of physics? Why go beyond nature?
objections.reply: Apply the chapter’s own test: does the candidate have any **potentiality**? The universe changes constantly, so it is shot through with potentiality. Mass-energy takes different forms at different times — it is potentially otherwise than it is. Fundamental particles and fields have states they could be in but aren’t. And laws, the chapter argues, are shorthand for how things with certain natures behave; they don’t exist on their own, and the question remains what makes it the case that things with *these* natures exist rather than others. Anything with potential needs an actualizer, so none of these can be the terminus. And whatever is purely actual must be immutable, eternal and immaterial — unlike anything physical.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘maybe the universe’s existence is just a brute fact’, point out that the argument doesn’t need the principle of sufficient reason; it needs only the principle that a mere potential can’t actualize itself. A brute-fact universe would be a vast collection of potentials actualized by nothing — the very thing Hume’s ‘pop into existence’ scenario tried and failed to make coherent.

objections.title: ‘God of the gaps’: science will eventually explain it
objections.whoRaises: Scientifically minded skeptics (a common modern objection)
objections.objection: Every time religion has pointed to something science couldn’t explain, science eventually explained it. The ‘sustaining cause’ is just another gap that physics will fill.
objections.reply: The argument doesn’t point to a gap in scientific knowledge; it points to something every scientific explanation **presupposes**. Science explains how things behave given that they exist with certain natures and follow certain laws. The Aristotelian question is what actualizes the existence of things with those natures here and now. Filling in more physics (a deeper particle, a new field) just adds more members to the hierarchical series — each with potentials needing actualization. No amount of physics can reach the terminus, because anything physical is a mix of act and potency. That is why Feser treats objections from physics as not even well-formulated: physics’ method abstracts from exactly what the argument is about.
objections.pushback: If they say ‘then the argument is unfalsifiable’, reply that it can be challenged the normal philosophical way — by attacking a premise or an inference, and many have tried. Being beyond the reach of experiments is not a defect; so are the laws of logic and the claim that only experiments yield knowledge.

misconceptions.myth: The argument claims the universe had a beginning and God started it.
misconceptions.correction: Feser explicitly grants, for argument’s sake, that the universe or a multiverse might have no beginning. The argument concerns what keeps things in existence here and now, at every moment. The Big Bang is irrelevant to it.

misconceptions.myth: The argument rests on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: Its principle is that whatever goes from potential to actual needs an actualizer. What is purely actual has no potential, so it neither needs nor could have a cause. ‘What caused God?’ attacks a straw man.

misconceptions.myth: ‘First cause’ means the cause that came first in time.
misconceptions.correction: In a hierarchical series, ‘first’ means having underived, built-in causal power, as opposed to the borrowed, instrumental power of the other members. It is first in the order of dependence, not in chronology.

misconceptions.myth: The argument commits the fallacy of composition by inferring that the universe as a whole needs a cause.
misconceptions.correction: No premise is about the universe as a whole. It starts from any single object — a stone, a cup of coffee — existing now. That the conclusion applies to everything is a consequence, not a premise.

misconceptions.myth: If the regress of causes were infinite, there would be no need for a first cause.
misconceptions.correction: True of linear series, but not hierarchical ones. An infinite series of instruments is as powerless as one instrument (an infinitely long brush handle, mirrors with no face). The need for a primary cause has nothing to do with the series being finite.

misconceptions.myth: The argument depends on Aristotle’s outdated physics.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on the metaphysical analysis of change as actualization of potential, not on geocentrism, the four elements or natural places. Science itself presupposes change (observation involves one experience following another), so no scientific theory can refute it.

misconceptions.myth: Because quantum events are indeterministic, they are uncaused.
misconceptions.correction: Causation doesn’t require determinism, only intelligibility. Lead-210 decays according to its nature (formal cause), was generated by something (efficient cause), and is kept in existence by something now. Scientists even call decay the ‘production’ of mercury-206.

misconceptions.myth: Even if there is an Unmoved Mover, it’s just an impersonal force, not God.
misconceptions.correction: Stage 2 argues that a purely actual cause must be one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, fully good, omnipotent and — via proportionate causality — intelligent and omniscient. The argument goes far beyond a bare ‘first cause’.

misconceptions.myth: A cause must change in order to cause anything, so a purely actual cause is impossible.
misconceptions.correction: That generalizes from the limited causes we observe — a fallacy of accident, like concluding no one over seven feet tall could be president. Our causes change as they act because they are limited (an arm is here and only potentially there). Pure act has no such limits, and the idea isn’t self-contradictory.

misconceptions.myth: The hierarchical series depends on causes being perfectly simultaneous, which physics and relativity rule out.
misconceptions.correction: What makes a series hierarchical is derivative, instrumental power, not simultaneity. Anyway, ‘simultaneous’ need not mean ‘instantaneous’: immediate causes are parts of the same event as their effects, at the same place, so relativity of simultaneity for distant events doesn’t apply.

misconceptions.myth: God’s sustaining the world means God is a physical force, like gravity, holding the atoms together.
misconceptions.correction: Physical forces are themselves members of the hierarchical series, with potentials of their own. Pure actuality is immaterial and outside time; it is the source of the being and power of all forces, not one more force among them.

misconceptions.myth: The argument assumes the medieval idea that every moving body needs something continuously pushing it.
misconceptions.correction: Feser notes that not all medieval Aristotelians held that, and Aquinas allowed some motion to follow ‘spontaneously’ from a thing’s nature. In any case the argument ultimately concerns what sustains a thing’s existence, not what keeps it moving.

explain.tweet: Change = potential made actual, and no potential actualizes itself. Your coffee exists right now only because its potential to exist is actualized now, by a hierarchy of causes that must end in pure actuality: one, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing. That’s God.
explain.elevator: Things change, and change means a potential becoming actual — which only something already actual can bring about. Now forget the past. Ask what keeps your coffee existing right now: the water depends on its molecules, those on atoms, those on particles, all at this very moment. Every link has borrowed existence, like a desk that holds a cup only because the floor holds the desk. A chain of borrowers needs a lender with nothing borrowed: pure actuality. And pure actuality turns out to be one, changeless, timeless, and all-powerful. That’s what we mean by God.
explain.twoMinute:
Start with something nobody denies: things change. Coffee cools. Even if you think you’re dreaming, your thoughts change. Aristotle explained change as a thing’s **potential** becoming **actual**. The hot coffee isn’t cold, but it *can* be cold in a way it can’t become chicken soup. And here’s the key: a potential can’t actualize itself, because what’s merely potential isn’t there yet to do anything. So anything that goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to make it so.

Now here’s where people usually go wrong. This is **not** about tracing causes back to the Big Bang. Grant that the universe has always existed. The question is about **right now**. What makes your coffee exist this second? It exists because its water exists; the water exists because its molecules are holding together as water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen; that depends on the atoms, and the atoms on subatomic particles — all simultaneously. Each layer has its existence only on loan from the layer beneath it, like a cup held up by a desk held up by a floor.

That kind of series — a **hierarchical** series — can’t go on forever without a source, because every member is only passing along what it received. An infinitely long paintbrush handle still can’t move itself. So there must be something that can actualize the existence of other things **without needing its own existence actualized** — something with no potentiality at all. **Pure actuality.**

Then notice what follows from pure actuality. It can’t change, since change is actualizing potential. So it’s outside time, and it isn’t material. It lacks nothing, so it’s perfect and fully good. There can’t be two of them, because nothing could distinguish them. Every power anything has flows from it, so it’s all-powerful. And since it causes every kind of thing, the patterns of all things must be in it the way ideas are in a mind — so it is intelligent and knows everything.

One, eternal, immaterial, all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good cause of everything, keeping it all in existence right now. That’s not a god of the gaps. That’s the God of classical theism.
explain.eli12:
Imagine a stack of books on a table. The top book stays up because the book under it is holding it. That book stays up because the one under it is holding *it*. None of the books is holding itself up. If there were nothing solid at the bottom, the whole stack would fall — even if the stack were a million books tall! Adding more books doesn’t help, because every book is just passing on the holding-up it gets from below.

Now think about you. You exist right now because your body’s cells are working right now. The cells exist because their molecules are holding together right now. The molecules exist because their atoms are, and the atoms because of even tinier particles. It’s like the stack of books: each layer is ‘held up’ in existence by the one underneath, all at the same time.

So there has to be something at the very bottom that isn’t held up by anything — something that just *is*, all by itself, and holds everything else up. It can’t be something that can change or break or wear out, because anything like that would need something else holding it up too. It has to be totally complete, with nothing missing.

That’s what people mean by God: not a big person sitting somewhere in space, but the one thing that holds everything else in existence every second, without needing anything to hold it.
whiteboard: Write ‘CHANGE’ and draw a hot coffee cup → cold cup. Ask: does anyone deny this happens? Note that even denying it involves a change of mind.
Under it write ‘ACT’ and ‘POTENCY’. List what the coffee can become (cold, spilled) and can’t (chicken soup). Say: potential is real but not yet actual — that answers Parmenides.
Write the principle of causality in a box: ‘A potential is actualized only by something already actual.’ Stress: NOT ‘everything has a cause’.
Draw a HORIZONTAL arrow chain: button → air conditioner → cool air → cold coffee, and extend it off the board with ‘…∞?’. Say: fine, grant this could be infinite. The argument concedes it.
Draw a VERTICAL stack at one moment: cup / desk / floor / foundation / earth. Label each upward arrow ‘borrowed power’. Explain per se vs per accidens.
Replace the stack with the real one: coffee / water / molecules / atoms / particles / ??? — label it ‘existence, right now’.

Draw an infinitely long paintbrush (or mirrors with no face) and cross it out: more instruments don’t add up to a source. At the bottom of the vertical stack write ‘PURE ACTUALITY — actualizes without being actualized’.

Draw spokes out from ‘PURE ACTUALITY’: no potency → immutable → eternal → immaterial; no privation → perfect, good; nothing to differentiate → one; source of all power → omnipotent; contains forms of all things → intelligent, omniscient.
Finish by writing the three misreadings to avoid in the corner: ‘not about the Big Bang’, ‘not about the universe as a whole’, ‘not everything has a cause’.
explain.keyAnalogy: The best analogy is Feser’s own **cup held up by the desk held up by the floor** (or, for existence, a **movie image that exists only while the projector is shining**). Use it to show two things at once: (1) a hierarchical series operates *now*, not back in time — knock out the floor and the cup falls at once, not in a billion years; (2) every intermediate member has only *borrowed* power, so adding more members — even infinitely many — never gives you a source. Then make the crucial swap: replace ‘height off the floor’ with ‘existence’. Just as the cup’s height depends at every moment on what holds it, the coffee’s very existence depends at every moment on the molecules, atoms and particles that make it up, and those on something further. Close the analogy honestly: the earth isn’t truly ‘first’ (it has potentials too), which is exactly why the real first cause must be something with no potentiality at all.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes this argument click is the difference between **a chain stretched out in time** and **a stack of dependence at a single moment**. Almost everyone hears ‘first cause’ as ‘the cause at the start of the timeline’, and then naturally replies, ‘Why couldn’t the timeline be infinite?’ or ‘Maybe the Big Bang had a natural cause.’ Feser agrees those points don’t matter. The argument is about what is making things exist *right now*, and that is a stack of *borrowed* causal power, where each layer only passes on what it is receiving.

Once someone sees that a stack of borrowers can’t explain itself, however tall it is, the need for an unborrowed source becomes intuitive. Once they also see that the source can’t have *any* potentiality — or it would just be another borrower — the divine attributes follow almost automatically.

The usual reason it fails to click is that the presenter says ‘everything has a cause’ or starts with the beginning of the universe. Both put the listener on the wrong track before the real argument has started.

audiences.startingPoint: Trusts physics as our best account of reality; suspects metaphysics is idle speculation; may think quantum mechanics or inertia has refuted ‘every change has a cause’.
audiences.approach: Start on their turf: ask what physics explains, and what it presupposes. Physics tells you how things with certain natures behave under certain laws; it never tells you why things with *those* natures exist here and now. Use the metal-detector and black-and-white drawing analogies to show that physics’ silence about causes is built into its method, not a discovery about nature. Then walk down the ladder of existence (coffee → water → molecules → atoms → particles) and ask what, at the bottom, is not itself a mix of act and potency. Handle quantum mechanics by distinguishing causation from determinism (Dowe’s lead-210 bucket).
audiences.openingQuestion: Physics tells us how things behave given the laws. What, in physics, explains why there are things with exactly those natures existing at this very moment?
audiences.avoid: Don’t pit the argument against a scientific theory (Big Bang, evolution) or suggest science is ‘missing something’ it could discover. Present it as a question physics’ method isn’t designed to answer, not a gap it might fill.

audiences.startingPoint: Has heard the cosmological argument as ‘everything has a cause, so God’, and is confident ‘What caused God?’ refutes it.
audiences.approach: Take the objection seriously and head it off early. Say up front: the argument doesn’t say everything has a cause — only that whatever goes from potential to actual needs an actualizer, and explain why. Then show that the exemption for God follows from the principle’s own logic. Emphasize that Aristotle’s argument predates Christianity and was formulated this way from the start, so it isn’t a trick invented to escape modern critics.
audiences.openingQuestion: Can something that is only potentially hot make itself actually hot — without anything already hot, or already energetic, acting on it?
audiences.avoid: Don’t get defensive or treat the ‘What caused God?’ question as stupid. It is a good objection to a bad version of the argument; say so, and show them the better version.

audiences.who: Philosophy student who knows Hume and Kant
audiences.startingPoint: Believes Hume showed causation is just constant conjunction and uncaused beginnings are conceivable; believes Kant confined causality to experience.
audiences.approach: Engage the actual arguments. On Hume: separate conceiving A without conceiving B from conceiving A existing without B (trilateral/triangle), and give Anscombe’s ‘transport vs. coming-to-be’ point. On Kant: the principle rests on the nature of potentiality, not on experience as such (Euclid in black ink). Then introduce the per se / per accidens distinction as a classic scholastic tool they may have missed, and ask them to evaluate the three-way dilemma for an ‘unmoved but not unmovable’ mover.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you imagine a brick appearing out of nowhere, what makes it a case of the brick coming into existence rather than being transported from somewhere?
audiences.avoid: Don’t pretend the attribute derivations are uncontroversial; say they get a fuller defense later. Overclaiming loses this audience fast.

audiences.who: Religious believer who wants to understand their faith
audiences.startingPoint: Already believes in God, may think of God mainly as the one who started the universe long ago, or as a very powerful being among others.
audiences.approach: Show how this argument deepens their idea of God: God isn’t just the one who lit the fuse at the Big Bang but the one who holds everything in existence at every moment, more intimately than any other cause. Explain why God is not ‘a being’ alongside others but pure actuality — immutable, timeless, simple. Point out how this defends against ‘what caused God?’ and against God-of-the-gaps thinking.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God stopped doing whatever he is doing right now, would the universe carry on for a while like a wound-up clock, or would it simply vanish?
audiences.avoid: Don’t let them assume the argument proves every doctrine of their tradition, or that it depends on the universe having a beginning. Keep it philosophical.

audiences.who: Agnostic who thinks these questions can’t be settled
audiences.startingPoint: Sympathetic but suspicious of any claim to ‘prove’ God; thinks it’s all speculation beyond human reach.
audiences.approach: Keep the starting points humble and undeniable (change occurs; mere potentials can’t actualize themselves) and let them see each step. Use Socratic questions so they reach the per se series and the need for a first member themselves. Emphasize that the argument doesn’t claim to picture God, only to infer what must be true of whatever sustains things — mostly by saying what it *cannot* be (changing, temporal, material, limited).
audiences.openingQuestion: Is there anything we can know for certain about the world? What about the fact that things change?
audiences.avoid: Don’t rush to the conclusion or use loaded words early (‘God’, ‘creator’). Say ‘unactualized actualizer’ until the attributes have been derived.

audiences.who: Physicist or engineer with little philosophy
audiences.startingPoint: Thinks in mechanisms and models; may object that desks are really particle clouds and that simultaneity is relative.
audiences.approach: Use their own practice. Engineers happily say a foundation supports a building without mentioning particle collisions; the particle story is the mechanism, not a refutation. Translate the hierarchical series into their terms (a load path, a power supply chain where each stage needs current from the one before). Then point to existence rather than support, and ask which level of the physical hierarchy lacks all potential. Mention that immediate causes are parts of the same event at the same place, so relativity of simultaneity doesn’t bite.
audiences.openingQuestion: In a power grid, every transformer passes on current it receives. What would happen if there were infinitely many transformers but no generator?
audiences.avoid: Don’t lean on examples that invite technical nitpicks without flagging that the details affect *how* the concepts apply, not *whether*.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So your argument is: everything has a cause, the causes can’t go back forever, so God started it all. Standard first-cause stuff.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Actually, no to all three parts. It doesn’t say everything has a cause, it doesn’t deny the causes could go back forever, and it’s not about starting anything.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what’s left?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Change. Your coffee is cooling. Aristotle says that’s a potential becoming actual — the coffee could be cold, and now it is. And a potential can’t make itself actual; something already actual has to do it, like the cooler air.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, but that’s just a chain back through time. Air cooled by AC, AC turned on by me, me born from my parents… and maybe it goes back forever. The universe might be eternal.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Grant it. Aristotle thought the universe was eternal. That kind of chain — where each link acts on its own, like the AC running after you leave — might have no first member. The argument’s about a different kind of series.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Which is?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The kind that works at this very moment. Your mug is up there because the desk holds it, now; the desk because the floor holds it, now; and so on. None of those has the power on its own — each passes on support it’s getting. Now apply that to existence. The coffee exists right now because its water does; the water because its molecules hold together as water rather than hydrogen and oxygen; that because of the atoms; that because of subatomic particles.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And you’re going to say that stack has to end. But why? Maybe it’s turtles all the way down.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because each member only has borrowed power. An infinitely long paintbrush handle still can’t move itself. Infinitely many mirrors reflecting each other still need a real face somewhere. If every layer is only passing along existence it receives, you need something that has it without receiving it — something with no potential that needs actualizing. Pure actuality.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, but then what caused *that*? If God doesn’t need a cause, why does the universe?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because the principle was never ‘everything needs a cause’. It’s ‘whatever goes from potential to actual needs a cause’. The universe is changing constantly, so it’s full of potential. Something purely actual has no potential — nothing in it to be actualized. It’s not an exception to the rule; it’s what the rule itself points to.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That sounds like a convenient redefinition to dodge the obvious question.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s how Aristotle put it 2,300 years ago, before anyone was asking about the Christian God — and it comes straight from his analysis of change. Besides, even if my motives were bad, that wouldn’t make the principle false.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s a better one. Quantum mechanics. Radioactive atoms decay for no reason. Particles pop out of the vacuum. So potentials get actualized with nothing actualizing them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Cause doesn’t mean deterministic cause. A lead-210 atom has some chance of decaying because of what lead-210 *is* — its nature. If I put a bucket of it in your room and you got sick, you’d rightly blame me, even though decay is probabilistic. And physics is a mathematical representation; not showing a cause isn’t the same as showing there’s no cause — like a black-and-white sketch of a sunset.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient again. Whatever physics says, you’ll say it’s ‘just a representation’.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Not whatever. Physics is great at what it measures. My point is only that its method leaves out certain things by design — like a metal detector and wood. And notice the quantum vacuum isn’t nothing; it’s a field with a definite nature. Something still has to account for a field with *that* nature existing right now.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Say I grant a first actualizer. It could just be some cosmic force, not God. Why the big theological leap?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because of what ‘pure actuality’ entails. No potential means it can’t change. If it can’t change, it isn’t in time and isn’t material. It lacks nothing, so it’s perfect and good. There can’t be two, because nothing could distinguish them. Every power anything has comes from it, so it’s all-powerful. A ‘cosmic force’ has states it could be in but isn’t — so it’s not the first actualizer.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And intelligence? That’s the part I really don’t see.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have in some way. It causes every kind of thing, so it has the forms of all things — not by *being* a cat or a tree, but the way you have the idea of a triangle without becoming triangular. Having forms that way just is what intellect is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Last try: to cause something you have to change. So a changeless cause is a contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The causes we observe change when they act — but that’s because they’re limited. My arm is here and only potentially there, so it has to move to move the stick. Concluding every cause must change is like concluding no one over seven feet could be president because none has been. And nothing contradictory is in ‘something that actualizes without being actualized’.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not converted. But I admit that’s not the argument I thought I was arguing against.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s all I wanted. If you want to reject it, pick the premise you think is false — the one about potentials not actualizing themselves, or the one about borrowed power needing a source — and we can look at that.

socratic: Is it possible to argue that change is unreal without your own thoughts changing as you argue?
Before the coffee cools, is its coldness nothing at all? Could it instead become chicken soup? What does that difference tell you?
Can something that is merely potentially hot make itself actually hot? What would it use to do that?
If you switch on an air conditioner and then leave, does it stop cooling the room? If the floor under your desk vanished, would your mug stay put? What’s the difference between those two cases?
Would a paintbrush with an infinitely long handle be able to move itself? Why or why not?
What keeps the water in your glass existing as water at this very second — not how it got there, or what could destroy it, but what makes it water right now?
If every layer of reality only has existence ‘on loan’ from the layer beneath, what would have to be true of whatever is at the bottom?
If something had no potential at all, could it change? Could it be in time? Could it be made of parts or of matter?
How could we tell two things apart if neither had any feature the other lacked?
Can you give someone $20 if you don’t have it in any way at all — not in cash, not in credit, not in the power to get it?
When you picture a stone suddenly appearing, have you pictured it having no cause — or have you just not pictured its cause?
Does a black-and-white photograph show that the world is colorless? What does that suggest about physics’ silence on causes?

traps.fix: State the real principle: whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual. Explain why potentials can’t self-actualize before anyone asks about God.

traps.trap: Framing the argument around the Big Bang or a beginning of the universe.
traps.fix: Concede an infinite past up front. Say the argument is about what sustains things right now, and draw the horizontal versus vertical series to make the difference visible.

traps.trap: Saying ‘the chain can’t be infinite’ without explaining why.
traps.fix: Explain the instrumental, borrowed-power character of per se series and use the infinite brush handle or mirrors. The point isn’t that infinity is impossible; it’s that borrowed power needs a lender.

traps.trap: Using the cup-and-desk example and then getting stuck in physics nitpicks (particles, time lags).
traps.fix: Say up front that the example only introduces the concept; move quickly to the existence series (water → molecules → atoms → particles), where timing doesn’t matter.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there’s a first cause’ and then just calling it God.
traps.fix: Derive at least three or four attributes from pure actuality before using the word ‘God’ — especially unity, immutability, and intelligence via proportionate causality.

traps.trap: Treating the earth (or the universe, or energy) as the first cause in the examples.
traps.fix: Point out, as Feser does, that the earth isn’t really first — it has potentials. The first cause must have none; that’s why no physical thing qualifies.

traps.trap: Dismissing scientific objections as irrelevant without explaining why.
traps.fix: Give the actual reason: physics’ mathematical method leaves out causal and qualitative features, so its silence is uninformative (drawing without color, metal detector). Then show causation isn’t determinism.

traps.trap: Overclaiming certainty about every attribute derivation.
traps.fix: Acknowledge Feser presents Stage 2 as a sketch defended more fully later. Invite the listener to challenge a specific step.

connections.note: The introduction sets out the book’s approach — rigorous, classical arguments that don’t depend on a beginning of the universe or on ‘God of the gaps’ reasoning. This chapter is the first and clearest example of that approach.

The Neo-Platonic proof runs a structurally parallel argument from composition instead of change: composite things depend here and now on something absolutely simple. The Aristotelian step ‘a first actualizer can’t have parts mixing act and potency’ anticipates it.

The Augustinian proof reaches a divine intellect from abstract objects (universals, propositions, possibilities). It complements this chapter’s route to divine intelligence via proportionate causality and the forms of things existing in their cause.

The Thomistic proof applies the same hierarchical (per se) sustaining-cause logic to the distinction between essence and existence, arriving at something whose essence just is existence. Pure actuality and subsistent existence turn out to be the same reality described two ways.

The Rationalist proof relies on the principle of sufficient reason, which is broader than this chapter’s principle of causality. Comparing the two helps you see that the Aristotelian argument needs only the weaker claim that potentials can’t actualize themselves.

The first part of the chapter on the nature of God returns to the principle of proportionate causality introduced here and gives the full defense of attributes only sketched in Stage 2 — unity, simplicity, immutability, immateriality and incorporeality, eternity, necessity.

The second part of the chapter on the nature of God completes the list (omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, will, love) and develops ‘conservation and concurrence’ — the sustaining causation at the heart of this proof — along with the Thomistic view of laws of nature this chapter invokes against the inertia and quantum objections.

The objections chapter takes up general objections to first-cause arguments that this chapter postpones: the ‘everything has a cause’ straw man and its history, quantum-physics objections, and the New Atheist critiques (Dawkins, Krauss, Hawking).

The second half of the objections chapter answers scientism — the claim that science is the only source of knowledge — which underlies the ‘outdated science’ and physics-based objections answered here, and shows how science rests on metaphysical foundations.

In the capstone, the Aristotelian proof serves as the anchor for comparing all five arguments: most of them share its structure of a per se regress ending in something that is not itself composite, limited, or dependent.

quiz.q: According to Aristotle, as Feser presents him, what is change?
options: Something coming into being out of nothing
The rearrangement of unchanging atoms
The actualization of a potential
An illusion produced by the senses
quiz.explanation: Change is a potential being made actual. A is Parmenides’ analysis, which Aristotle rejects: a potential is not nothing, as you can see from the fact that coffee can grow cold but cannot turn into a chicken. B is atomism, which still has to say what actualizes the new arrangement.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that denying the reality of change is self-refuting?
options: Reasoning to a conclusion is itself a change in the mind
Parmenides contradicted himself about the coffee’s coldness
Aristotle refuted it by experiment and observation
The senses perceive change directly and cannot be doubted
quiz.explanation: Working through premises to a conclusion is a succession of mental states, so the very act of arguing that change is unreal presupposes change. D is tempting but is not Feser’s reply here: he grants for the sake of argument that the senses might be deceiving us, and shows that change would still occur.

quiz.q: Which statement is the principle of causality as the chapter formulates it?
options: Everything that exists has a cause of its existence
Every event is necessitated by some prior event
Whatever begins to exist has a cause of its beginning
Any actualized potential is actualized by something already actual
quiz.explanation: The principle concerns only what goes from potential to actual, which is why nothing purely actual falls under it. A is the straw man behind ‘What caused God?’; B confuses causation with determinism, which Feser denies; C is the kalām premise, which needs the universe to have begun.

quiz.q: Which of these is a linear (per accidens) causal series?
options: A lamp hanging from a chain attached to a ceiling fixture
Al begets Bob, who later begets Chuck
A cup held up by a desk held up by a floor
A stone moved by a stick moved by a hand
quiz.explanation: Bob can beget Chuck whether or not Al is still alive: relative to the others, each member’s causal power is his own. The other three are Feser’s hierarchical examples, where each intermediate acts only while it is itself being acted on.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what fundamentally makes a causal series hierarchical?
options: All of its members exist at the same instant of time
Every member but the first has only derivative, instrumental power
It has only finitely many members, however long
It stretches backward in time without a beginning
quiz.explanation: Simultaneity (A) is how Feser introduces the idea and is the tempting answer, but he says explicitly that it is not what makes such a series hierarchical. What matters is the borrowed character of the intermediate members’ power — which is why an infinitely long one (C) would still need a source.

quiz.q: In a hierarchical series, the ‘first’ cause is first in the sense of…
options: coming earliest in time
being number one in a finite list
being the largest or most powerful member
having underived, built-in causal power
quiz.explanation: ‘First’ means primary in the order of dependence. A and B are the everyday senses of the word and are exactly what Feser is warning against: even an infinitely long hierarchical series, with no earliest member and no end to the count, would still need a cause with non-derivative power.

quiz.q: A friend says: “Cosmologists think there might be an eternal multiverse, so there is no need for a first cause.” What is the best reply from this chapter?
options: It already grants a beginningless universe and asks what sustains things now
The Big Bang shows the universe must have had a beginning
An actually infinite past is mathematically impossible
Aristotle himself proved that the universe must have begun
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly concedes an infinite linear series for the sake of argument. B and C are the moves a kalām defender would make, not this argument; and D is simply false — Aristotle held that the world had always existed.

quiz.q: What point does the infinitely long paintbrush handle illustrate?
options: No infinite series of any kind is possible
The brush must have been made by someone in the past
Adding instruments never supplies the underived power to move them
Motion always takes some amount of time
quiz.explanation: The handle’s length is irrelevant, because wood has no built-in power of movement. A is the tempting misreading, but Feser is explicit that Aristotelians accept infinite mathematical series and even beginningless linear causal series.

quiz.q: Asked what keeps the water in the coffee in existence, someone answers: “A chemical reaction bonded the hydrogen and oxygen a while ago.” What is Feser’s response?
options: That gets the chemistry of water wrong
That is circular reasoning in disguise
That already presupposes the existence of God
That explains how the water got here, not what keeps it in being
quiz.explanation: The argument asks about the cause of being at each moment, not the cause of becoming in the past. The parallel error runs the other way too: ‘nothing has come along to split it’ explains how the water might cease, not what sustains it. Nothing in the reply disputes the chemistry (A).

quiz.q: Why can there be only one purely actual actualizer?
options: The universe has room for only one first cause
Telling two apart would require an unactualized potential
Two such beings would inevitably come into conflict
Ockham’s razor forbids multiplying entities
quiz.explanation: Things of a kind are told apart by material or temporal features, or by some perfection one has and the other lacks — and every one of those implies an unrealized potential or a privation, which pure act cannot have (steps 15–18). D is tempting because it also yields ‘just one’, but a rule of thumb about theory choice is not what the chapter argues.

quiz.q: In the $20 example, having money in the bank and writing a check illustrates possessing the effect in the cause…
options: formally
eminently
virtually
accidentally
