quiz.explanation: Virtually means having the power to get hold of it. Formally would be having the $20 bill in hand; eminently would be the higher power of causing such bills to exist at all, as in the Congress scenario. The distinction matters because the cause of cats need not itself be a cat.

quiz.q: Why does Stage 2 conclude that the purely actual actualizer has intellect?
options: The forms of all it causes must be in it, as they are in an intellect
The order and design of the universe point to a designer
Only an intelligent person could be the cause of anything
Omnipotence already includes knowledge of everything
quiz.explanation: The route runs through proportionate causality (step 38) plus what intellect is: having a thing’s form without being that kind of thing. B is a design argument, which this chapter never uses. D reverses the order: omniscience is derived after intellect, from the fact that the forms of all things are in it.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, does ‘What caused God?’ fail as an objection?
options: Only what goes from potential to actual needs a cause
God is the cause of his own existence
Questions about God’s cause are meaningless ones
Causes could not exist before time itself began
quiz.explanation: What is purely actual has no potential to be actualized, so it falls outside the rule entirely — and the exemption follows from the rule’s own rationale, which is why it is not special pleading. B is the most tempting wrong answer and is not Feser’s view at all: a self-caused thing would have to exist before itself. Pure act is uncaused, not self-caused.

quiz.q: Against Hume, Feser notes that we can conceive of a trilateral without thinking of it as a triangle. What does this show?
options: Geometry is known a priori, not from experience
Some shapes cannot be imagined at all
Conceiving A without B is not conceiving A as existing without B
Trilaterals are the cause of triangles
quiz.explanation: No trilateral could exist without being a triangle, even though we can think of the one without the other. So imagining a stone appearing without imagining its cause is not imagining it as having no cause — which is all Hume’s thought experiment actually delivers.

quiz.q: Feser answers Kant by comparing the principle of causality to Euclidean geometry learned from black-ink diagrams. The point is that…
options: geometry, like causation, rests entirely on sense experience
a principle learned from experience can reach beyond experience
causation is a category that the mind imposes on the world
only things we could observe can have causes
quiz.explanation: Things need causes not because we experience them but because they are potential until made actual, and that ground is completely general. A is tempting because we do learn both from experience, but how we learn a principle does not fix how far it reaches — geometry applies to figures of any colour and of none.

quiz.q: What is the main point of the metal-detector analogy used against Russell?
options: Physics is unreliable about the world
Metal is the most fundamental kind of stuff
Russell’s equations were themselves mistaken
A method’s success says nothing about what it cannot detect
quiz.explanation: Physics captures only what can be mathematized, so its silence about causation is an artifact of method, not a discovery about the world. A and C overshoot: Feser never disputes either the reliability of physics or Russell’s mathematics.

quiz.q: According to the chapter, a law of nature such as inertia is best understood as…
options: an independently existing force that governs matter
a regularity with no further ground
shorthand for how things tend to behave given their natures or forms
a direct decree of God overriding nature
quiz.explanation: A law is a description of how a thing with a certain nature will act, so laws presuppose the existence of things with such natures and cannot explain it. B is the popular alternative, but it leaves unanswered the question the chapter presses: why are there things of this sort rather than another?

quiz.q: Feser says quantum theory approximates ‘potentiality without actuality’. What does the block universe approximate?
options: Potentiality without change
Causality without determinism
Determinism without causality
Actuality without potentiality
quiz.explanation: The block universe treats all moments as equally actual, leaving no potential to be actualized. Since causation is the actualization of a potential, a picture missing either half leaves causation out — which is Feser’s point about both theories.

quiz.q: In analyzing the decay of lead-210, which of the following is NOT one of the causes Feser identifies?
options: A deterministic trigger fixing the exact moment of decay
A formal cause: the atom’s nature
An efficient cause that generated the atom
A deeper efficient cause keeping the atom in existence now
quiz.explanation: The whole point is that the decay is indeterministic and still caused: its nature grounds the probability, something generated it, and something sustains it now. Looking for a hidden deterministic trigger (A) concedes the objector’s assumption that only necessitating causes are causes.

quiz.q: Why does Feser insist that ‘simultaneous’ does not mean ‘instantaneous’?
options: Relativity makes simultaneity relative to a frame
A cause’s acting and the effect can be one event that takes time
All causes act in a single indivisible instant
Hume proved that causes must precede their effects
quiz.explanation: Pushing a chair across a room takes time, yet there is no gap between the pushing and the chair’s being pushed: they are one event. A is the related but different objection from relativity, which Feser answers separately — it concerns spatially separated events, not two aspects of one event in one place.

quiz.q: Someone objects: “Mathematics has infinite series that work perfectly well, so why can’t a hierarchical causal series be infinite?” How does Feser reply?
options: Infinite mathematical series are impossible too
A mathematical series involves no instrumental and primary causes
Mathematics is merely a useful human invention
Aquinas already refuted infinite series explicitly
quiz.explanation: Aristotelians do not reject infinite series as such; they accept infinite mathematical series and even beginningless linear causal series. What cannot go on forever is a series of instruments with nothing whose instruments they are. Feser makes the same complaint about Graham Oppy, who says Aquinas gives no reason to rule out an infinite series while ignoring the role instrumental causality plays in the argument.

quiz.q: In the ‘unmovable mover’ discussion, suppose the first actualizer had a purely actual part that actualized its potential part. What does Feser conclude?
options: That purely actual part would be the true first actualizer
The first actualizer would be self-caused
There would be two gods
A vicious regress would result
quiz.explanation: The merely potential ‘part’ would not be part of the first actualizer at all, but rather the first of its effects. D is the right answer to a different branch of the same dilemma — the one where the actualizing part is itself a mixture of act and potency.

quiz.q: Someone argues: “Every cause we have observed changes when it acts, so any cause whatever must change.” Which fallacy does Feser say this commits?
options: Special pleading
Ad hominem
Composition
Accident
quiz.explanation: It treats a contingent feature of the causes we happen to have met as if it were essential to being a cause — like inferring that no one over seven feet could be president because no president has been. Composition (C) is tempting but concerns inferring from parts to wholes, which this argument does not do.

quiz.q: Which scholastic terms correspond to Feser’s ‘linear’ and ‘hierarchical’ series?
options: Formal and efficient
Virtual and eminent
Per accidens and per se
Potential and actual
quiz.explanation: A linear series is ordered per accidens (accidentally), a hierarchical series per se (essentially), as Feser notes in a footnote citing Aquinas and Scotus. ‘Accidentally ordered’ does not mean random: it means the ordering is not essential to each member’s power to act.

quiz.q: Which step of the formal argument makes the crucial move from a thing’s changes to its very existence at a moment?
options: Step 4
Step 7
Step 11
Step 38
quiz.explanation: Step 7 says that a substance’s existence at any moment presupposes the concurrent actualization of its potential for existence — the move that turns an argument about change into an argument about being. Step 4 is the principle of causality, step 11 rules out an infinite hierarchical regress, and step 38 is proportionate causality.

quiz.q: Which principle does Stage 2 add in order to establish divine intelligence, which Stage 1 did not need?
options: The principle of proportionate causality
The principle of sufficient reason
The principle of causality
Ockham’s razor
quiz.explanation: Step 38 adds proportionate causality: whatever is in an effect is in its cause formally, virtually or eminently. C was already doing the work in Stage 1, and B is the principle the Rationalist proof of Chapter 5 uses — the Aristotelian proof deliberately needs only the narrower claim.

quiz.q: A student says: “Maybe the first cause does have potentials — it just isn’t using them right now.” What is Feser’s reply?
options: Any way of actualizing it either demotes the cause or restarts the regress
Potentials that are never actualized are not real potentials
We cannot know anything about the first cause’s inner nature
An unused potential would violate Newton’s law of inertia
quiz.explanation: The dilemma has three branches: something else actualizes the potential (so this is not the first actualizer), a purely actual part does (so that part is the real first cause), or a mixed part does (so the regress starts again). B is not Feser’s view — unactualized potentials are perfectly real, which is the whole point of the coffee’s potential coldness.

quiz.q: “The universe might be eternal, so no first cause is needed.” Which distinction does this objection ignore?
options: Formal vs. eminent possession of an effect
Linear (per accidens) vs. hierarchical (per se) series
Qualitative vs. quantitative change
Formal vs. efficient cause
quiz.explanation: An eternal universe concerns a linear series running back through time, which Feser explicitly grants might have no beginning. The argument rests on the hierarchical series holding things in existence now, which cannot be beginningless because its members have no power of their own.

quiz.q: “The equations of physics never mention causes, so causes do not exist.” Which distinction does this objection ignore?
options: Absence from a representation vs. representation of absence
Linear (per accidens) vs. hierarchical (per se) series
An unmoved mover vs. an unmovable mover
Virtual vs. eminent possession of an effect
quiz.explanation: A method that omits something by design gives no evidence that the thing is missing from reality — as a black-and-white drawing is no evidence that the scene was colourless. Feser adds that the same reasoning would abolish events, laws and variables.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to: “In the quantum vacuum, particles come into existence out of nothing”?
options: Quantum field theory is simply false here
Virtual particles are illusions of measurement
God creates each particle by a separate miracle
The field itself may be the cause; silence is not evidence
quiz.explanation: Following Pruss, the system described by quantum field theory can be the cause, indeterministically; and a vacuum is a structured physical system with laws, not nothing at all. The deeper point is methodological: a description that abstracts from causality will never display causality. C is the god-of-the-gaps move the chapter is at pains to avoid, and A concedes far more than Feser needs.

quiz.q: Feser says even the earth is not a ‘first’ cause in the strict sense. Why not, given the rest of the chapter?
options: The earth is itself moving through space at speed
The earth came into existence at a particular time
The earth too has potentials, including its potential for existence
The earth is too far from the cup to act on it directly
quiz.explanation: A strictly first cause actualizes without being actualized in any respect. The earth, like the water in the coffee, exists at each moment only because potentials of its constituents are being actualized, so it is one more dependent member of the series. A and B name real facts about the earth, but neither is the reason: a cause could be moving or recent and still be first if its power were underived.

quiz.q: A tree whose roots are damaged cannot take in enough water. In the chapter’s terminology, this is…
options: a privation
a negation
an eminent cause
a substantial change
quiz.explanation: A privation is the absence of something a thing’s nature requires — a proper potential left unrealized. A negation (B) is merely lacking what is not proper to you, as a stone lacks sight; that is why the damaged tree counts as defective and the stone does not.

quiz.q: What is Anscombe’s point against Hume’s claim that we can conceive of something beginning to exist without a cause?
options: Causes always come before their effects in time
The imagination is an unreliable guide here
Hume was not really an empiricist at all
Telling coming-to-be from transport requires causes
quiz.explanation: Hume needs the cup appearing in empty space to count as coming into being rather than being moved there from elsewhere — and only the kind of cause involved distinguishes the two. So the very scenario meant to eliminate causation has to smuggle it back in.

quiz.q: On Weisheipl’s analysis, which Feser adopts, the principle of inertia is…
options: proved by experiment and observation
refuted by relativity theory
assumed by mathematical physics, not proved by it
a special case of the principle of causality
quiz.explanation: The mathematician must equate quantities, so he treats steady motion as the baseline needing no explanation and quantifies only changes in it. A is the natural assumption and is exactly what Weisheipl denies: physics assumes the principle, and so can neither affirm nor deny the causal realities it abstracts from.

quiz.q: What is Richard Healey’s point, as Feser uses it against the block universe?
options: Relativity itself proves that change is real after all
Denying all change is incoherent: physics rests on change
Time is an illusion produced by human consciousness
Simultaneity turns out to be absolute after all
quiz.explanation: Observation and experiment involve going from one experience to another, so a theory denying all change would undercut its own evidence. Note how modest the conclusion is: the most one could coherently claim is that change is confined to the mind — and even that is enough actualization of potential for the argument to start.

quiz.q: What does Phil Dowe’s example of the bucket of lead-210 show?
options: Radioactive decay is really deterministic after all
Indeterministic links still count as causal
Moral responsibility is an illusion
Mercury is more dangerous than lead
quiz.explanation: If only deterministic links were causal, then bringing the bucket in would not have caused your radiation sickness, and so I could not be morally responsible for it — which is absurd. Dowe adds that scientists themselves describe such decay as the production of mercury, and production is near enough to causation.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say the Eddington-style objection is raised ‘selectively’?
options: No one faults engineers or doctors for talking the same way
Only theists ever use everyday examples
Eddington later withdrew the whole view
Physics does not really apply to furniture
quiz.explanation: Engineers talk about foundations supporting buildings and doctors about disks supporting the spine, and nobody calls that outdated science. Feser also makes a deeper point: even if physics did conflict with the commonsense description, the examples only illustrate the concepts and could be restated in terms of particles.

quiz.q: Feser uses Mumford and Anjum’s example (sugar dissolving, tea drunk, tea digested) to show that…
options: all causes are simultaneous with all of their effects
causes always precede their effects in time
one process only sets up the conditions for the next
sugar has dispositional properties of its own
quiz.explanation: Causation within a process is simultaneous, but separate processes are linked by condition-setting rather than by that same kind of causation — so chains of events through time do not collapse into one instant. A is the objection this answers: if every cause were simultaneous with its effect, all of history would seem to happen at once.

quiz.q: What is the endless series of mirrors reflecting a face meant to show?
options: Mirror images are ultimately illusions
Mirrors are instrumental causes of faces
Actual infinities are impossible in reality
Even an endless series needs an underived source outside it
quiz.explanation: However many mirrors pass the image along, there must be an actual face somewhere supplying it — what there cannot be is only reflections and never a face. C is the misreading Feser explicitly disowns: his claim is about borrowed power, not about the impossibility of infinity.

quiz.q: In the Al–Bob–Chuck footnote, what is the most important sense, according to Feser, in which none of them has inherent causal power ‘full stop’?
options: Each inherited the power to beget from his own parents
Each of them will eventually grow old and die
Each came into existence at a particular time
None could act unless his body’s matter were actualized now
quiz.explanation: Feser mentions inheritance (A) as one sense but says the most important is present dependence on hierarchical series. That is exactly why every stage of a linear series presupposes hierarchical series, and why granting a beginningless line of ancestors costs the argument nothing.

quiz.q: Someone says, “God is just the biggest and most powerful thing in the universe.” Which correction follows from the chapter?
options: God is as large as the whole universe put together
God is a kind of infinitely extended matter
God is not a thing among things but pure actuality itself
God is the first event in the history of the cosmos
quiz.explanation: Pure actuality is immaterial and eternal, so it is not an item within the universe at all, however large or powerful. D repeats the picture the chapter sets aside: this cause is first in rank, not first in time.

quiz.q: To deny divine unity, which step would a critic most directly have to reject?
options: Step 1
Step 16
Step 38
Step 49
quiz.explanation: Step 16 claims that a differentiating feature would require an unactualized potential; reject it and two purely actual beings might be distinguishable after all. Step 38 is the principle of proportionate causality, which is used later to derive intellect, not unity.

shortAnswer.q: Explain how Aristotle’s distinction between actuality and potentiality answers Parmenides’ argument against change.
shortAnswer.model: Parmenides argued that change would require something to come from nothing — the coffee’s coldness doesn’t exist while it is hot, so if the coffee cools, coldness arises from nothing, which is impossible. Aristotle replies that the coldness wasn’t simply nothing: it existed **potentially**. The coffee has a real, determinate capacity to become cold (unlike a capacity to become chicken soup). Change is the **actualization** of such a potential, so nothing comes from sheer nothingness. Feser also notes that denying change is self-refuting, since reasoning is itself a change.
rubric: States Parmenides’ something-from-nothing argument
Defines potentiality as real but unactualized, not nothing
Uses an example showing potentials are determinate (can/can’t become)
Defines change as actualization of potential

shortAnswer.q: Why does the principle of causality follow from the nature of potentiality rather than being a mere generalization from experience?
shortAnswer.model: A potential is, by definition, not yet actual. What is not actual can’t do anything — only what actually exists can act. So a potential can’t make itself actual: if it could, it would already have to be actual, which contradicts its being merely potential. Therefore every actualization requires something already actual. Experience confirms this abundantly, but the principle rests on what potentiality is, which is why it can be applied beyond experience (Feser’s reply to Kant).
rubric: Potential = not yet actual
Only the actual can act/cause
So no potential actualizes itself
Notes this grounds the principle’s generality beyond observed cases

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish linear and hierarchical causal series, giving an example of each, and explain why only the hierarchical kind must have a first member.
shortAnswer.model: In a **linear (per accidens)** series, each member has its own causal power relative to the others and can keep acting after earlier members are gone — the air conditioner keeps cooling after you leave; Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive. Nothing in such a series requires tracing any member’s activity back to a first, so it could be beginningless. In a **hierarchical (per se)** series, every member except the first has only borrowed, instrumental power and acts only while being acted on — the desk holds the cup only while the floor holds the desk. Borrowed power must come from something that has it unborrowed; otherwise nothing in the series could act at all. Even an infinite series of instruments (an infinitely long brush handle) would need a primary cause.
rubric: Correct linear example and characterization (inherent power, can outlast predecessors)
Correct hierarchical example and characterization (derived/instrumental power, concurrent dependence)
Explains that linear series need no first member
Explains that borrowed power requires an underived source regardless of length

shortAnswer.q: Explain the move from the changes a thing undergoes to the thing’s existence at a moment. Why is this move so important?
shortAnswer.model: Change presupposes a thing that changes: coffee can cool only if it exists. So Feser asks what keeps the coffee — or its water — in existence right now. The water’s matter could exist as separate hydrogen and oxygen; its being water now is an actualized potential. Past causes explain how it came to be, and the absence of disruptors explains how it might cease, but neither explains what makes it water now. Chemical bonds and atomic structure only push the question down a level. This reveals a hierarchical series of actualizers of existence. The move matters because it makes the argument independent of time: it doesn’t depend on a beginning of the universe, on the timing of causes, or even on the reality of change in the physical world (e.g., the block universe).
rubric: Change presupposes an existing substance
Existence now is an actualized potential (water vs. separate gases)
Distinguishes cause of becoming / ceasing from cause of being now
Identifies a hierarchical series of existence
Explains why this shields the argument from beginning/timing/block-universe objections

shortAnswer.q: Why must the first actualizer be purely actual — unmovable, not just unmoved?
shortAnswer.model: The first actualizer is first because it actualizes others’ existence without its own existence being actualized. If it had any potential needing actualization in order to exist, something would have to actualize it: (1) something else — then it isn’t first; (2) a purely actual part of itself — then that part is the real first actualizer and the potential part is merely its first effect; or (3) a part that is itself mixed act and potency — which would need its own actualizer, restarting a vicious regress. So any genuine first actualizer of existence must be purely actual, and hence has all the attributes that follow from pure actuality.
rubric: Frames the issue as the actualization of existence
Presents the three-way dilemma accurately

shortAnswer.q: Derive the attributes of immutability, eternity and immateriality from pure actuality.
shortAnswer.model: Change is the actualization of potential; what is purely actual has no potential, so it can’t change — it is **immutable**. Existing in time entails changeability (succession, before and after), so an immutable being isn’t in time — it is **eternal** in the sense of timeless, without beginning, end or succession. Being material entails changeability and temporality, so what is immutable and eternal is **immaterial**, and so also **incorporeal**, having no body.
rubric: Immutability from no potential + definition of change
Eternity as timelessness from immutability
Immateriality from matter entailing change and time
Incorporeality from immateriality

shortAnswer.q: Explain the principle of proportionate causality, using the $20 example, and show how Stage 2 uses it to establish divine intelligence.
shortAnswer.model: What is in an effect must be in its cause somehow, since a cause can’t give what it lacks. I can give you $20 only if I have it **formally** (a twenty in my wallet), **virtually** (credit in the bank I can draw on), or **eminently** (the higher power to print twenties). The purely actual cause is the cause of everything that exists or could exist; to cause a thing is to cause something of a particular form (a cat, a tree). So the forms of all things must be in the cause — not formally (it isn’t a cat) but eminently, and in a universal, abstract way, since it causes every possible instance. Having forms abstractly without being those things is exactly what intellect is. Since it also causes the relations among things (this cat on this mat), these pre-exist in it as combinations of forms, like thoughts or a craftsman’s plans. So it is intelligent — and, since nothing lies outside its thoughts, omniscient.
rubric: States the principle (cause can’t give what it doesn’t have)
Correctly explains formally/virtually/eminently with the $20 cases
Cause of everything → forms of everything in it
Forms present abstractly/universally = intellect
Notes omniscience follows

shortAnswer.q: What is wrong with the objection ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ Include Feser’s response to the charge that the argument’s formulation is ad hoc.
shortAnswer.model: The argument never says everything has a cause; it says whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause. That difference is like the difference between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all figures have three sides’. And the exemption for God isn’t arbitrary: things need causes because they have potentials, and pure actuality has none, so it neither needs nor could have a cause. Against the ad hoc charge: (1) motives don’t refute arguments (that would be ad hominem); (2) historically, Aristotelians from Aristotle through Aquinas to today have always stated the principle this way; (3) it follows naturally from the analysis of change, independent of theism.
rubric: Correct statement of the real principle
Explains why the exemption follows from the principle’s rationale
Mentions the triangle analogy or equivalent
Gives the three replies to the ad hoc charge

shortAnswer.q: Summarize Feser’s general strategy for answering objections from physics (Russell, inertia, relativity, quantum mechanics).
shortAnswer.model: Mathematical physics deliberately confines itself to what can be described mathematically — a ‘partial consideration’ of nature. That is the source of its predictive success, but it guarantees physics will omit qualitative and causal features such as potentiality. So **absence from the representation is not a representation of absence** (a black-and-white drawing doesn’t show a colorless scene; a metal detector doesn’t show there’s no wood). Moreover, laws of physics describe how things with certain natures behave, so they presuppose the existence of such things and can’t explain what sustains them. Science also presupposes change in the scientist’s experience. Hence these objections affect at most how the principle of causality applies, not whether it does. Specific points: causation isn’t determinism (quantum); the block universe’s existence would still need an actualizer; inertia is assumed by mathematical physics, not proved.
rubric: Physics as mathematical abstraction / partial consideration
Absence from representation ≠ representation of absence (with an analogy)
Laws presuppose natures and existing things
Science presupposes change in experience
At least two specific applications (quantum determinism, block universe, inertia, Russell)

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser defend the reality of hierarchical causal series against the objection that there are no truly simultaneous causes?
shortAnswer.model: First, simultaneous doesn’t mean instantaneous: a cause’s acting and the effect’s being acted on are one event, however long it lasts (pushing a chair). Second, immediate causes are always simultaneous with their effects: it is the billiard ball’s impact, not its earlier motion, and the brick’s pressing into the glass, not the throw, that immediately causes the effect (Mumford and Anjum). Third, this doesn’t collapse all causal chains into one instant, because we must distinguish causation within a process from one process setting up conditions for another (sugar dissolving, tea drunk, tea digested). Fourth, relativity of simultaneity concerns separate events at different places, not a cause and effect that are parts of one event at one place. Finally, simultaneity isn’t what makes a series hierarchical anyway — derivative power is — and the key series concerns existence at an instant.
rubric: Simultaneous ≠ instantaneous
Immediate causes simultaneous with effects (an example)
Within-process vs. condition-setting distinction
Relativity irrelevant (same event, same place)
Hierarchy defined by derivative power / existence at an instant

shortAnswer.q: Present Feser’s three replies to Hume’s claim that something could begin to exist without a cause.
shortAnswer.model: (1) Hume only shows we can imagine a thing appearing **without also imagining its cause**, not that we can conceive of it **having no cause**. Conceiving of A without B is not conceiving of A existing without B: a trilateral can be thought of without thinking ‘triangle’, and a man without his height, but neither can exist that way. (2) Following **Anscombe**, Hume must say why the scenario is a case of coming into existence rather than transport from elsewhere, and only the kind of cause marks that difference, so causation re-enters. (3) The principle is **massively confirmed by experience**. We find causes when we look and reasonably assume them when we can’t (unsolved crimes). If it were false, anything could pop up anywhere (Clarke’s elephant or hotel), and constantly. The best explanation is that potentiality by nature needs an actualizer.
rubric: Distinguishes conceiving without a cause from conceiving no cause, with an analogy
States Anscombe’s coming-into-existence vs. transport point
Gives the empirical argument (causes found; things don’t randomly appear)
Draws the inference to the best explanation

shortAnswer.q: Explain the argument for divine unity (steps 15–18) and why material and temporal differences are not available to distinguish purely actual beings.
shortAnswer.model: Two things of a kind can be two only if something distinguishes them, some feature one has that the other lacks. Ordinarily we distinguish things by material or temporal features (larger, taller, here vs. there, earlier vs. later), but pure actuality is immaterial and eternal, so none of those apply. More generally, things of a kind differ by some perfection or privation one has and the other lacks (sturdier roots, a missing tail). But any such difference would mean one of them lacks some actuality, which is an unrealized potential, and pure act has none. So nothing could differentiate two purely actual beings, and there is exactly one.
rubric: States the need for a differentiating feature
Explains why material/temporal features are ruled out (immaterial, eternal)
Explains why perfection/privation differences imply potentiality
Concludes uniqueness

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser respond to the claim that Einstein’s block universe shows change is an illusion?
shortAnswer.model: He doesn’t need to settle whether the block interpretation is correct (it is controversial). (1) Denying all change is **incoherent**: physics rests on observation and experiment, making predictions and then testing them, going from ignorance to knowledge, all of which is change (Richard Healey). At most one could say change exists only in the mind, but change in the mind is still actualization of potential, enough to start the argument. (2) Even with no change anywhere, a thing’s very **existence** involves actualized potential, so the block universe as a whole would still need an actualizer distinct from it, a cause of this world rather than another being actual. So relativity affects how, not whether, the principle of causality applies.
rubric: Describes the block-universe objection accurately
Gives the self-undermining / evidence point
Notes that change in the mind suffices
Gives the existence-of-the-block point
Concludes ‘how, not whether’

shortAnswer.q: Analyze radioactive decay (e.g., lead-210) in Aristotelian terms, as Feser does, and explain why it doesn’t refute the principle of causality.
shortAnswer.model: Lead-210 behaves according to its **nature or form**, as copper conducts electricity and dogs chase squirrels. Its nature includes a probability *x* of decaying in the next minute. So the decay is **indeterministic but intelligible**, grounded in what lead-210 is (its **formal cause**). It also has an **efficient cause** in whatever generated the atom, and, most importantly, a deeper efficient cause in whatever keeps it existing **now** as lead-210 rather than something else or nothing. That actualized potential still needs a purely actual actualizer. Dowe adds that indeterministic links still ground responsibility (the bucket of lead-210) and that scientists call decay the ‘production’ of mercury-206. The objection only works if we conflate causation with deterministic causation.
rubric: Nature/form grounds the probability (formal cause)
Distinguishes intelligibility from determinism
Names the generating efficient cause and the sustaining cause
Uses at least one of Dowe’s points (bucket, ‘production’)

shortAnswer.q: Why can a hierarchical series not be infinite, even though Aristotelians accept infinite mathematical series and possibly beginningless linear series? Include the two objections Feser rebuts here.
shortAnswer.model: In a linear series each member has causal power inherently relative to the others (Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive), so nothing requires tracing activity back to a first member. In a hierarchical series each member acts only by power imparted from outside, so without a member with **underived** power we just pass the explanatory buck. An instrument must be the instrument of something, and length is irrelevant: an infinitely long brush handle still can’t move itself, and endless mirrors still need a real face. **Oppy’s** appeal to infinite mathematical series fails because such series involve no instrumental and primary causes, indeed no causation. **Sobel’s** charge of begging the question fails because calling a cause ‘instrumental’ says only that its power is derived. Whether a regress of derived powers must end is argued, not assumed; even a skeptic sees a stick can’t move a stone on its own.
rubric: Contrasts inherent (linear) vs. derived (hierarchical) power
Explains buck-passing / instrument of nothing, with brush or mirrors
Rebuts the mathematical-series objection
Rebuts the begging-the-question objection

shortAnswer.q: Why does Feser deny that the Aristotelian argument rests on outdated science? Address both the sweeping version and the Eddington version of the objection.
shortAnswer.model: **Sweeping version:** ‘Aristotelianism’ labels a huge range of ideas. Specific scientific theses (geocentrism, the four elements, natural places) were refuted, but the metaphysical thesis that change is actualization of potential was not. Science actually presupposes it, since observation involves passing from one experience to another. The book’s arguments rest on these deeper metaphysical foundations. **Eddington version:** the claim that a desk is really a particle cloud doesn’t conflict with its holding up the cup; it gives the mechanism. The objection is raised selectively (engineers and doctors aren’t accused of outdated science), and the details are irrelevant anyway, since the examples only introduce concepts (actualization, linear vs. hierarchical) that apply at any level of description, affecting how, not whether, they apply. Compare how no one faults a physicist’s ride-a-light-beam thought experiment.
rubric: Separates refuted scientific theses from the metaphysical thesis
Notes that science presupposes change/actualization
Mechanism vs. competition point on Eddington
Selectivity point
Irrelevance point (how, not whether)

flashcards.front: What is change, on Aristotle’s analysis?
flashcards.back: The actualization of a potential — something potentially F becoming actually F.

flashcards.front: Four kinds of change (with Feser’s examples)
flashcards.back: Qualitative (coffee cools), local (leaf falls), quantitative (puddle grows), substantial (swatted fly dies).
Change would require something, such as coldness, to come from nothing — which is impossible. So change cannot occur.
(1) Self-refuting: reasoning your way to the conclusion is itself a change. (2) Aristotle: what comes to be was already there potentially, and a potential is not nothing.
It is determinate: coffee can grow cold or stain the rug, but it cannot become chicken soup or a live chicken.
Any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. (NOT ‘everything has a cause’.)

flashcards.front: Why can’t a potential actualize itself?
flashcards.back: Because what is merely potential is not actual, and only what is actual can do anything.

flashcards.front: Does every changer have to be changing?
flashcards.back: No. The rule is only that IF a changer is itself changing, its change needs a changer too.

flashcards.front: Linear (per accidens) series — definition and example
flashcards.back: Members strung out in time, each with its own power relative to the others; e.g. button → AC → cool air → cold coffee. Could have no beginning.

flashcards.front: Hierarchical (per se) series — definition and example
flashcards.back: Every member but the first has only derived, instrumental power and acts only while acted on; e.g. earth → foundation → floor → desk → cup. Must have a first member.

flashcards.front: What does ‘first’ mean in ‘first cause’ here?
flashcards.back: Having underived, built-in causal power — not earliest in time, and not first in a count.
It still could not move itself: adding instruments never yields underived power. The length is irrelevant.

flashcards.front: What happens to a linear series, and to a hierarchical series, when an earlier member is removed?
flashcards.back: Linear: the air conditioner keeps cooling after you leave the house. Hierarchical: if the floor collapses, desk and cup fall with it.

flashcards.front: Why is the hierarchical series ‘more fundamental’?
flashcards.back: Things can change only if they exist, and their existing at each moment depends on a hierarchical series of actualizers.

flashcards.front: What keeps the water in the coffee existing now?
flashcards.back: Not what produced it in the past, and not the absence of anything splitting it — something must be actualizing its matter’s potential to exist as water at this very instant.
Feser’s precise name for the Unmoved Mover: something that actualizes other things without being actualized — pure actuality.

flashcards.front: Does the argument need a beginning of the universe?
flashcards.back: No. Feser grants a possibly infinite past, as Aristotle believed; the argument is about what sustains things now.

flashcards.front: Does the argument assume the universe as a whole has a cause?
flashcards.back: No. It starts from any single thing. Applying the result to everything is a consequence, not a premise.
Only what goes from potential to actual needs a cause. Pure act has no potential, so it neither needs nor could have one.

flashcards.front: Triangle analogy (against the ‘no real difference’ rejoinder)
flashcards.back: Equating ‘whatever goes from potency to act has a cause’ with ‘everything has a cause’ is like equating ‘all triangles have three sides’ with ‘all figures have three sides’.

flashcards.front: Three replies to the ‘ad hoc’ charge
flashcards.back: (1) Motives cannot make a claim false — that is ad hominem. (2) It is historically false: the claim has been put this way since Aristotle. (3) It follows from the analysis of change anyway.
Conceiving A without conceiving B is not the same as conceiving A existing without B (trilateral and triangle; a man without a height).
What makes a sudden appearance a coming-into-existence rather than a transportation? Only the kind of cause — so causation sneaks back in.
We learn geometry from black-ink diagrams, yet it applies to figures of any colour; likewise causality applies wherever there is potential, observed or not.
If the principle of causality were false, things could pop into existence anywhere at any time — and they do not.
Proves too much (Schaffer); particles have dispositions (Martin); other sciences and naturalism rely on causation; physics is not exhaustive (the later Russell).

flashcards.front: Metal detector, the easy-A student, the drunk under the streetlamp
flashcards.back: A method’s success with what it is built to find tells you nothing about what it cannot detect.
It concerns events in time, not existence; laws presuppose natures; and mathematical physics assumes inertia rather than proving it (Weisheipl).

flashcards.front: Two replies on the block universe
flashcards.back: (1) Denying all change is incoherent — science rests on changing experiences (Healey). (2) The block’s own existence would still need an actualizer.
A cause must make its effect intelligible, not necessary. Indeterministic causation is still causation.
Absence from a representation is not a representation of absence — and in a colour hold the lines even let you infer the contour that only colour will supply.
Quantum: potentiality with nothing shown actualizing it — Heisenberg called the probabilities ‘potentia’. Block universe: actuality with no potentiality. Either way causation drops out.
Formal (its nature, grounding the probability); efficient (whatever generated it); deeper efficient (whatever keeps it in existence now).
If indeterministic links were not causal, I would not be responsible for your radiation sickness — which is absurd.
Whatever is in an effect is in its cause formally, virtually or eminently; a cause cannot give what it does not have.
Twenty in the wallet / credit in the bank / the power to print twenties.
Grasping universal concepts, combining them into thoughts, and reasoning from thought to thought. The first is the most fundamental.

flashcards.front: Why only one purely actual being?
flashcards.back: Differentiating two would need some feature or privation one lacks — that is, an unactualized potential, which pure act cannot have.

flashcards.front: Unmoved vs. unmovable: the three-way dilemma
flashcards.back: A potential in the first actualizer would be actualized by (1) something else — so it is not first; (2) a purely actual part — so that part is first; (3) a mixed part — so the regress restarts.

flashcards.front: Fallacy of accident (in the unmovable-mover section)
flashcards.back: Inferring that all actualizers must change because the observed ones do — like concluding that no seven-footer could be president.
Any change presupposes a substance that undergoes it: there is no cooling without something that cools.

flashcards.front: What does step 7 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: A substance’s existence at any moment requires its potential for existence to be actualized at that moment — its matter could have been otherwise.

flashcards.front: Steps 9–10: the two options for the actualizer A
flashcards.back: Either A’s own existence is being actualized, starting a regress of concurrent actualizers, or A is purely actual.

flashcards.front: What does step 11 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: A regress of concurrent actualizers is hierarchical and so cannot be infinite, because borrowed power needs an unborrowed source.
Whatever exists in time can change; pure act cannot change; so it exists outside time.
Being material entails being changeable and in time, so pure act is immaterial and therefore incorporeal.
Every actualization comes from pure act directly or through a series ending in it — so all power derives from it (omnipotence).
Forms exist either concretely in things or abstractly in an intellect; they cannot be in pure act concretely, so they are there as in an intellect.
For there to be a single purely actual cause with these attributes just is for God to exist.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘a first cause isn’t God’ → reply
flashcards.back: Stage 2 derives the divine attributes from pure actuality alone, so the argument reaches far more than a bare cause.
No premise concerns the universe as a whole; the argument starts from any single thing.
Particles describe the mechanism of support, not a refutation of it — and no one raises this against engineers or doctors.

flashcards.front: Objection: there are no simultaneous causes → reply
flashcards.back: Simultaneous does not mean instantaneous: an immediate cause and its effect are one event, however long it lasts.

flashcards.front: Objection: infinite series cannot be ruled out (Oppy) → reply
flashcards.back: Aristotelians reject only a series of instruments with no source of power; mathematical series involve no instrumental causes at all.

flashcards.front: Objection: calling causes ‘instrumental’ begs the question (Sobel) → reply
flashcards.back: ‘Instrumental’ means only ‘derives its power from another’; that the regress must end is then argued, not assumed.

flashcards.front: Objection: a purely actual actualizer is incoherent → reply
flashcards.back: The objection begs the question, commits a fallacy of accident, and points to no contradiction of the ‘immortal mortal’ kind.
The refuted theses (geocentrism, natural place) are scientific; act and potency is metaphysics, which science presupposes.

flashcards.front: Distinction: cause of becoming vs. cause of being
flashcards.back: Becoming: what originally produced a thing (the brewing). Being: what keeps it in existence now. The argument concerns being.
Privation is lacking what your nature requires (a blind dog). Negation is lacking what is not proper to you (a stone’s lack of sight).
Pure act is uncaused, since there is nothing in it to actualize — not self-caused, which would require existing before itself.
Prime matter depends on form and form on matter, so the composite would be an explanatory circle unless something outside it holds it in being.

flashcards.front: Why ‘chemical bonding’ doesn’t answer what keeps water in existence
flashcards.back: It restates the question: the atoms could be bonded otherwise, so why this way, now? Appealing to atomic structure only pushes it down a level.

teachBack:
**Your challenge:** Explain the Aristotelian proof, out loud, to a smart friend who has never studied philosophy and who believes the universe may be eternal. You have **ten minutes** and one sheet of paper.

**Constraints:**

- You may not say ‘everything has a cause’ or mention the Big Bang except to set it aside.
- You must use one hierarchical example (the cup on the desk, or your own) and one linear example, and say clearly why only one needs a first member.
- You must make the move from change to existence using the water example (water → molecules → atoms → particles).
- You must derive at least **four** divine attributes from pure actuality, including **unity** and **intelligence**.
- Before you finish, invite your friend to ask ‘What caused God?’ and answer it in under 30 seconds.

**Check yourself afterward:**

1. Could your friend repeat, in their own words, the difference between a linear and a hierarchical series?
2. Did you explain *why* a hierarchical series can’t regress infinitely (borrowed power), rather than just asserting it?
3. Did you distinguish ‘first in time’ from ‘first as underived’?
4. Did you avoid overclaiming? (Stage 2 is a sketch; Feser defends the attributes fully later.)
5. Where did you hesitate or reach for jargon? Those are the places to reread — usually the principle of proportionate causality and the unmovable-mover dilemma.

Then repeat the exercise in **three minutes**, and finally in **one sentence**.
videoPrompt: Audience: curious, intelligent adults with no philosophy background, including skeptics. Explain Edward Feser’s Aristotelian proof of God (Chapter 1 of Five Proofs). Emphasize, in order: (1) change is undeniable and means potential becoming actual (hot coffee can become cold, not chicken soup); (2) no potential actualizes itself; (3) the argument is NOT about the Big Bang — grant an eternal universe; (4) linear series (air conditioner keeps running after you leave) vs. hierarchical series (cup held by desk held by floor); (5) what keeps water existing right now — molecules, atoms, particles — must end in pure actuality; (6) why ‘first’ means underived, not earliest (infinitely long paintbrush, mirrors with no face); (7) how unity, immutability, eternity, perfection, omnipotence and intelligence follow. Correct these misconceptions: ‘everything has a cause’, ‘what caused God?’, ‘quantum mechanics shows causeless events’. Tone: clear, warm, rigorous, respectful of skeptics, never preachy.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This chapter tries to prove something, the way a geometry textbook proves something. Not *suggest*, not *make plausible* — prove. That is a bold thing to attempt, and it is worth knowing up front what the target is, because almost everyone brings the wrong picture to it.

Here is the wrong picture: long ago there was nothing, then God pushed a button, and the universe has been running ever since. Feser is not arguing for that. He says so explicitly, more than once, and still expects readers to misremember him. His argument would work fine even if the universe had always existed, with no beginning at all.

Here is the right picture. Look at something near you — a cup, a chair, your own hand. It exists right now. Feser is going to argue that its existing *right now, at this instant* is not a free-standing fact. It depends on something else, which depends on something else, and that chain of dependence — a chain running downward at this moment, not backward through history — has to stop somewhere. It stops, he argues, in something that does not depend on anything: something with no unrealised possibilities in it at all. Then, in the second half of the chapter, he argues that anything like that would have to be one, unchanging, outside time, without a body, perfect, good, all-powerful, intelligent and all-knowing — which is to say, what people have always meant by God.

What will you be asked to accept? Very little, and nothing religious. Essentially two things: that change really happens, and that nothing can give itself what it doesn't have. Everything else is supposed to follow.

A word about the hard parts. Two ideas do the heavy lifting: the difference between what a thing *is* and what it *could be* (Aristotle's actual and potential), and the difference between two kinds of causal chain — one stretching back through time, one holding things up right now. Get those two, and roughly eighty per cent of the chapter is downhill. If a page feels impenetrable, check whether it is really about one of those two ideas in disguise; usually it is. And the second half — the long stretch on Hume, Russell, Newton, Einstein and quantum mechanics — is defence, not offence. You can read it faster, or come back to it, without losing the thread.

knowFirst.plain: Anything becoming different in any way — coffee cooling, a leaf falling, a puddle spreading, a fly dying. Feser will treat all of these as one kind of event, and he will need only that at least some of them are real.
How a thing actually is right now. Your coffee is actually hot. Only things that are actual can do anything; a possibility can't reach out and make itself happen.
What a thing could become but isn't yet. Hot coffee can become cold; it cannot become chicken soup. That difference is real, and it is about the coffee — which is Aristotle's whole point.

Whenever a possibility becomes a reality, something already real made it happen. Note that this is not the claim that everything has a cause — a distinction that will matter enormously when the chapter reaches 'so what caused God?'

A chain running back through time: the coffee cooled because the room was cool, the room was cool because of the air conditioner, and so on. Each link keeps working after the one before it is gone. Feser is happy for this kind of chain to run back forever.

A chain holding something up right now: the cup rests on the desk, which rests on the floor, which rests on the foundation. Remove any link and the whole thing drops instantly. This is the kind of chain the argument is really about.
Something that only does its job because something else is working through it — the brush doesn't paint, the painter paints with it. The desk holds nothing up on its own; it is borrowing.
Not 'the earliest one' but 'the one that isn't borrowing'. This is the single most misunderstood word in the chapter: 'first' means first in rank, not first in time.

Something with nothing left over — no unrealised possibilities at all, nothing in it waiting to be brought about. It is where the argument's chain of dependence finally stops, and every divine attribute in the second half is squeezed out of this one idea.

What keeps a thing in existence from moment to moment, as opposed to what originally made it. The question 'what made this?' is about history; 'what keeps this here?' is the question the chapter cares about.

questionsToHold: Is Feser asking what started the universe, or what is holding it up right now? Watch how often he goes out of his way to say it is the second.
Why exactly can one kind of causal chain run backward forever while the other cannot? Try to state the difference in your own words before Feser states it for you.
When he says 'first cause', does he mean earliest, or does he mean something else? Underline every place he explains the word.
The argument never claims 'everything has a cause'. What weaker claim does it make instead — and does that really dodge the 'so what caused God?' objection, or is it a dodge?

In the second half, each attribute (unchanging, timeless, immaterial, one, good, all-powerful, intelligent) is squeezed out of a single feature. What is that feature, and does each squeeze really work?
Which of the scientific objections — Newton, Einstein, quantum mechanics — actually touches a premise of the argument, and which only touches an illustration Feser used?
At the end, ask yourself honestly: if you don't accept the conclusion, which numbered step is the one you reject? If you can't name one, that's worth sitting with.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1 (opening)
map.what: Change is real — coffee cooling, a leaf falling, a puddle growing, a swatted fly. Parmenides' ancient argument that change is impossible is raised and answered with Aristotle's actual/potential distinction. Then: change needs a changer, because a mere possibility can't make itself happen. Finally the everyday chain of causes running backward through time, and Feser's cheerful concession that it might run back forever.
map.tip: The friendliest pages in the chapter. Read them properly rather than skimming — the coffee, the leaf, the puddle and the fly come back again and again, and the actual/potential distinction introduced here carries the entire book. Note carefully that Feser grants a beginningless universe for the sake of argument; he is not going to need a beginning.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1 (the hierarchical series and what 'first' means)
map.what: The turn of the chapter. A second kind of causal chain is introduced: the cup held up by the desk, held up by the floor, held up by the foundation, held up by the earth. Nothing in that chain holds anything up under its own power — they are all instruments, like a brush in a painter's hand. That, Feser argues, is why this kind of chain must have a first member, where 'first' means having built-in power rather than coming earliest. Then a stock-taking paragraph that retraces the whole route so far.
map.tip: Slow right down here, and reread if necessary — if you understand only one stretch of this chapter, make it this one. Two things to nail: (1) what makes a chain hierarchical is borrowed power, not simultaneity; (2) 'first' means first in rank, not first in time. The infinitely long paintbrush handle is the image to memorise. The stock-taking paragraph at the end is a free checkpoint: if it doesn't sound familiar, go back.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1 (from change to existence)
map.what: Feser shifts from asking what makes things change to asking what makes them exist at this instant. The water in your coffee: the same matter could exist as loose hydrogen and oxygen, so its being water right now is a possibility being realised right now. Chemistry and atomic structure only push the question down a level. The chain must terminate in something with no potential for existence at all — pure actuality, an unactualized actualizer, Aristotle's Unmoved Mover.
map.tip: The hardest three pages in the chapter, and the pivot of the whole argument — read them twice, the second time slowly. The move to watch is Feser ruling out two tempting answers: 'someone brewed it' (that's history) and 'nothing has split it apart yet' (that's the future). Neither answers what keeps it water now. There is also a long footnote about hylemorphism, substantial form and prime matter — safely skipped on a first read; Feser says himself the argument doesn't need it.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 2
map.what: Why call this thing God? One after another, the traditional attributes are derived from the single fact of having no unrealised potential: unchanging, therefore outside time, therefore immaterial and without a body; perfect and fully good (because a defect is an unrealised potential — the injured squirrel, the damaged tree, the bad painter); one and only one; all-powerful. Then a slower stretch defining what intelligence is, introducing the principle that a cause can't give what it hasn't got (the $20 example), and concluding to intellect and omniscience.
map.tip: Read this as a sketch, not as a finished case — Feser says repeatedly that the divine attributes get a whole chapter of their own later on, so don't stall on objections here. The $20 example is the one to hold onto: the three ways of having something (in your wallet, in the bank, with the power to print it) is doing real work in the argument for divine intelligence.

map.section: A more formal statement of the argument
map.what: The whole thing laid out as fifty numbered lines, from 'change is a real feature of the world' to 'God exists'. Steps 1–14 are Stage 1; 15–18 give unity; 19–27 immutability, eternity, immateriality and incorporeality; 28–32 perfection and goodness; 33–37 omnipotence; 38–47 intelligence and omniscience; 48–50 the conclusion.
map.tip: Don't read this as prose — read it as a checklist against the pages you've just finished. For each numbered line, try to name the paragraph earlier in the chapter that defended it. The lines that carry the real weight are 4, 7, 9 and 11; the rest are either definitions or straightforward consequences. If you end up disagreeing with the chapter, this is the page where you should be able to point at a number.

map.what: Three misreadings cleared away: that the argument needs the universe to have had a beginning (it doesn't); that it assumes the universe as a whole needs a cause (it doesn't — one coffee cup is enough); and the famous 'if everything has a cause, what caused God?' (the argument never said everything has a cause, only that whatever goes from potential to actual does). Feser adds that this is not an ad hoc dodge — it has been the claim for twenty-three centuries.
map.tip: Easy, satisfying, and the most immediately useful pages in the chapter for arguing with real people. Learn the difference between 'everything has a cause' and 'whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause' well enough to say it out loud. Feser's comparison — that is like confusing 'all triangles have three sides' with 'all shapes have three sides' — is worth memorising.

map.what: Hume: we can imagine something popping into existence uncaused, so causation isn't necessary. Feser: imagining a cup appearing without picturing its cause is not the same as conceiving it as uncaused — and Anscombe's point that Hume can't even distinguish the cup appearing from the cup being moved there without smuggling causes back in. Then Kant: even if causation holds inside experience, why extend it beyond? Feser: because what grounds the principle isn't experience but the fact that a possibility can't realise itself.
map.tip: The trilateral/triangle example is the key to the Hume reply — conceiving of A without conceiving of B is not conceiving of A without B. For Kant, the geometry comparison does the work: we learn geometry from figures drawn in black ink, but what we learn isn't about black ink.

map.what: Russell argued that physics describes the world with equations that never mention causes, so causation is a relic. Feser gives four replies: it proves too much (equations don't mention events, laws or explanations either); physics does involve causal notions; other sciences certainly do; and — the deepest point — physics deliberately describes only what can be captured mathematically, so it cannot possibly be a complete description of reality. The later Russell is quoted admitting exactly this.
map.tip: The metal-detector image is the one to keep: a metal detector finds only metal, so its success proves nothing about whether non-metallic things exist. This section is really about the limits of physics rather than about causation, and it will come in handy far beyond this chapter.

map.what: Doesn't Newton's first law — a moving body keeps moving with no force acting — show that change can happen uncaused? Feser's reply distinguishes the question of what keeps a body moving from the question of what actualizes its potential to be at each new place, and appeals to the idea that some activity follows from a thing's own nature without a continuously conjoined external mover.
map.tip: Genuinely hard, and the place where physics and metaphysics are easiest to run together. The thing to hold on to: a law of physics describes a pattern; it does not by itself explain why the pattern holds or what is doing the actualizing. Feser notes he has treated this at length elsewhere, so the treatment here is compressed — don't expect it to feel complete.

map.what: If relativity shows that past, present and future are all equally real — the 'block universe' — then perhaps nothing really changes at all, and the argument loses its starting point.
map.tip: Short but conceptually slippery. The point to grasp is that the block universe is an interpretation of the physics rather than a result of it, and that in any case the deeper version of the argument doesn't need change over time at all — it can run on a thing's simply existing at one instant. If this section defeats you, note that and move on; nothing later depends on it.

map.what: The longest defensive stretch in the chapter. Three challenges: quantum indeterminism (events with no determining cause), the Bell inequalities, and particles appearing in a quantum vacuum. Feser answers each — different interpretations of quantum mechanics exist (the Copenhagen and de Broglie–Bohm readings differ on exactly this); a vacuum isn't nothing; Heisenberg himself compared quantum probabilities to Aristotle's potentiality. Radioactive decay gets extended treatment. The deeper reply is that being undetermined is not the same as being uncaused.
map.tip: The longest slog in the chapter, and you can read it at half attention on a first pass provided you take away one sentence: undetermined is not the same as uncaused. Come back to the details later if a sceptic actually presses you on quantum mechanics. Feser's real point isn't about physics at all — it's that a thing's own nature and structure produce its behaviour even when the timing isn't fixed.

map.what: The objection that the cup-desk-floor examples rest on a naive picture of solid objects, since Eddington's famous 'two tables' remind us that physics describes mostly empty space and colliding particles. Feser answers that the everyday description and the physical one are not competitors, that physics merely gives the mechanism, and that nobody raises this quibble against engineers or doctors. And anyway, the examples were only illustrating actuality, potentiality and the two kinds of causal chain — notions that apply however the physics turns out.
map.tip: A breather after the quantum section, and enjoyable. The point worth carrying away is the general one: an example can be scientifically naive while the idea it illustrates is untouched. Feser's black-hole comparison — nobody objects that photons are too small to sit on — makes it memorable.

map.what: Two serious objections. First: are there really simultaneous causes, given measurable time lags and relativity? Feser answers that simultaneous doesn't mean instantaneous — pushing a chair takes time, but there's no gap between your pushing and its being pushed — and that immediate causes are simultaneous with their effects while more remote ones aren't. Second, and more importantly: what makes a series hierarchical isn't simultaneity at all, but derived power. He closes by dismissing two misfiring objections — infinite mathematical series (no causation involved) and the charge of begging the question (calling a cause instrumental only means it borrows its power).
map.tip: Demanding but important, and the place where a careful reader's remaining doubts get answered — worth the effort. The big relief comes near the end: Feser concedes that simultaneity was only a teaching device, and that what really matters is borrowed versus built-in power. If you found the simultaneity discussion confusing, that concession lets you set it aside. The long footnote about Al, Bob and Chuck is genuinely helpful on why family trees are linear rather than hierarchical.

map.what: The last objection: granted there's a first actualizer, why must it be purely actual rather than merely something that happens not to be changing right now? Feser works through every version of the suggestion and shows each one either relocates the first actualizer or restarts the regress. He then answers the charge that a purely actual actualizer is incoherent — that objection assumes its own conclusion, and it commits the fallacy of accident, reasoning from how the actualizers we've met behave to how any actualizer must behave.
map.tip: A clean, tidy ending — read it properly rather than letting attention drift at the finish line. The presidents-under-seven-feet-tall example is the one to remember: every president so far has been under seven feet, but that doesn't make it a requirement of the office. Likewise, every actualizer we've met changes, but that doesn't make changing part of what it is to be an actualizer.

afterReading: Without looking at the book, say out loud in under a minute what the argument is. If the words 'in the beginning' or 'the Big Bang' come out of your mouth, you have the wrong argument — go back to pages 37–38.

Draw the two kinds of causal chain side by side on one sheet of paper: the coffee/air-conditioner chain going backward in time, and the cup/desk/floor chain going down right now. Label which one can run forever and write one sentence saying why.
Explain the word 'first', as Feser uses it, to an imaginary person who thinks it means 'earliest'. Use the paintbrush.

Take the water in your coffee and walk down the chain out loud: water, atoms, subatomic particles… At each level say what would happen if nothing were actualizing it, and notice what you are tempted to say instead.

Look at the fifty numbered steps again and pick the one you find least convincing. Write two sentences saying why, then find the pages in the chapter where Feser defends it. Did he anticipate your worry?

Say the difference between 'everything has a cause' and 'whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause' in one sentence, and then say why the difference means the argument isn't special pleading.

Pick any three of the divine attributes in Stage 2 and trace each one back to the single feature it was derived from. If you can't get from that feature to the attribute, mark it — that's where your own reading needs to go deeper.

Finally: tell someone who has never read a word of philosophy what the chapter argues, in about two minutes, using nothing but a coffee cup and a desk. Where they look confused is where you don't yet understand it.
